* feat(agent)!: expose portable model-turn termination metadata to hooks (#2184)

`on_model_turn_finished` could see what a turn produced but not why it
stopped. The reason was already normalized and already recorded on the
run — it simply terminated one frame short of the hook, so the one
policy every retry hook wants ("the provider cut this off, go again with
more room") was unreachable without reaching for `M::Response`, which is
what the hook's medium-neutral design forbids.

`ModelTurnFinished` gains two fields:

- `finish_reason: Option<&FinishReason>` — rig-core's existing normalized
  vocabulary rather than a new enum, so per-provider mappings and the
  verbatim `Other` fallback already apply, and `truncated_output()` is
  the same predicate rig-agent itself uses to decide whether an
  answerless turn is explicable. It is this attempt's own reason, after
  the `Stop`->`ToolCalls` reconciliation both surfaces apply. `None`
  means the provider reported no reason and is deliberately not smoothed
  into `Stop`: "finished normally" and "did not say" are different facts
  to steer on.
- `max_tokens: Option<u64>` — the cap this attempt was prepared with,
  after agent config, runner/request override, and the merged
  completion-call `RequestPatch`. Carried on `PreparedCompletionRequest`
  rather than read back off the agent, because the builder is consumed
  before the turn's hooks fire and the agent's baseline is not what a
  patched retry ran under.

Both surfaces read both values from the same per-attempt carrier, so
blocking and streaming cannot report different metadata for one turn.
No retry counters were added to agents, builders, runners, or run state:
a narrower policy limit stays the hook's, in the run-scoped scratchpad.

Adds a credential-free `retry_on_truncation` example whose scripted
model truncates as a function of the cap it is given, so the escalation
loop is causal rather than staged; it runs the same hook on both
surfaces and they produce identical traces.

Breaking only for code constructing `ModelTurnFinished` by hand (test

* test(agent): live cross-provider cassette matrix for turn termination metadata

The unit cells added with the feature drive a `MockCompletionModel`, so they
prove the agent plumbs whatever the model layer hands it — they cannot prove
that a provider's wire value *becomes* the normalized reason by the time a
hook sees it. That is the half of "normalized across providers" that had no
coverage.

24 recorded cells, 8 per provider: {Length, Stop, ToolCalls} x {blocking,
streaming}, plus an escalating retry on both surfaces. They replay real
OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini bytes through the provider mapper, the agent and
the hook stack.

What the recorded wire actually says, per normalized reason:

    normalized   openai(chat)  anthropic   gemini
    Stop         stop          end_turn    STOP
    Length       length        max_tokens  MAX_TOKENS
    ToolCalls    tool_calls    tool_use    STOP

Gemini is the reason this matrix earns its keep: it has no distinct tool-turn
wire value, so its recorded tool fixture says `"finishReason":"STOP"` and the
hook still observes `ToolCalls` because `reconcile_with_output` upgraded it.
That is the live proof of a reconciliation the unit cells could only mock, and
it is exactly what a portable retry hook would otherwise have to special-case.

`TurnTerminationProbe` and `EscalateCapOnTruncation` live in
`tests/common/support.rs` and are the same types all three suites drive — if a
provider had needed its own probe, the metadata would not be provider-neutral.

The six escalation cells each recorded two interactions: a real two-call round
trip where the first attempt truncated under a tiny cap, the hook read
`Length` off the event and asked for a repeat with a larger one, and the
second attempt reported its own cap rather than the agent's baseline of 64.

Every cell re-reads its own fixture and fails if the recorded turn stopped
carrying the wire reason the cell is about, so a provider changing behavior
breaks the cell instead of leaving it green while covering nothing. The retry
cells also assert the recorded request caps in order, which is what proves the
number the hook reported is the number that went on the wire.

Verified: recorded live against all three providers; replays with every
provider key unset (24/24, <0.6s per suite); mutation-checked twice — dropping
the reason from the event kills 24/24 cells, and reading `runner.config

escalation cells. All 24 fixtures scanned for org/project headers, user_id,
key material and emails: no matches.

ContentFilter, Other(_) and a provider reporting no reason are not live
recordable — the first has no benign trigger and the others no reachable
benign wire value on these endpoints. Each suite header says so; all three are
pinned by unit cells where the vocabulary can be enumerated without a live
call.

* fix(providers): report the page ceiling only when the loop hits it

`paginate_models` decided it had hit its page ceiling from

still holds the *previous* page's cursor whenever the listing ended
normally. Any listing past its first page therefore logged

         returning the pages fetched so far

on a complete, correct result -- telling an operator their catalog was
truncated at 1000 pages when three were fetched. The repeated-cursor
break emitted both warnings for one event.

This is not hypothetical. Anthropic's catalog fits one page today, but
Gemini's paginates in production (`/v1beta/models` returns 50 models plus
a `nextPageToken`), so every real Gemini listing would have warned.

The ceiling is now decided by loop exhaustion, which is what it means:
every `break` is the provider ending the listing, and only running out of
iterations is a bound rig imposed.

The regression cells live in their own test binary. `tracing` caches
callsite interest globally, computed by whichever thread reaches the
callsite first, while `set_default` installs a subscriber for one thread
-- so a sibling test emitting these same warnings without a subscriber
caches `Interest::never` and silences the capture mid-test. That is not a
hypothetical either: the assertions were flaky when they sat beside the
other listing tests. Alone in a binary and serialized by
`scoped_tracing_subscriber_guard`, nothing else reaches the callsites.

passes either way, so the fix cannot be "stop warning at all".

fix(embeddings): keep a document's embeddings in text order across batch boundaries (#2348)

* fix(embeddings): keep a document's embeddings in text order across batches

#2344 fixed the outer ordering of `build_with_usage` — the returned pairs now
follow input order. The inner `Vec<Embedding>` was still non-deterministic:
`chunks` splits on a flat text count, so one document's texts can straddle a
batch boundary, `buffer_unordered` yields batches as they finish, and
`acc.entry(i).or_default().push(embedding)` recorded completion order. A
straddling document got its own embeddings back shuffled — the same silent
mis-association #2344 fixed, one level down.

With `MAX_DOCUMENTS = 5`, a six-text document, and a model whose first batch is
slow, the old code returned `["t5", "t0", "t1", "t2", "t3", "t4"]`: the sixth
text's embedding at index 0. Since the derived `Embed` impl emits a struct's
fields in declaration order, a caller reading `embeddings[j]` as "field j" got
a neighbour's vector.

Both levels now fall out of one mechanism. Every text is assigned a global
slot index before chunking, each document records the contiguous slot range it
owns, and a finished batch writes each embedding into its own slot — so when a
batch completes cannot affect where anything lands. Reassembly hands each
document its run of slots in order.

Two consequences worth noting:

- A slot left empty means the provider returned fewer embeddings than the
  texts sent. `zip` used to drop the surplus silently and hand back a short
  list; the slot names the gap, so it is now a located error.
- A document that embeds no text still errors rather than returning an empty
  list, exactly as before. Pinned by a test, since the rewrite could easily
  have turned it into a silent empty vec.

The manual two-vector loop the follow-up issue suggested collapsing with
`unzip` is gone entirely — spans have to be computed in the same pass — and
the capacity pre-allocation it would have brought is now there.

Fixes #2345

* docs(changelog): record the embeddings inner-order fix (#2345)

* test(embeddings): invert every batch boundary, not just the first

Review of the ordering fix turned up four things worth correcting.

`SlowFirstBatchModel` delays only the *first* batch, so in the
four-document test doc3 straddled a boundary whose two batches still
arrived in submission order — it came back correct even unfixed, and
the test's coverage was one straddle rather than two. Both boundaries
now invert under `DescendingLatencyModel`, and on unfixed main doc1 and
doc3 return `["t2","t0","t1"]` and `["t1","t2","t0"]` respectively.

Two more shapes the span arithmetic should survive: one text per batch
finishing backwards, and documents that tile `MAX_DOCUMENTS` exactly so
every document boundary is also a batch boundary.

The comment on the `get_mut` write claimed it guarded against a provider
answering with more embeddings than it was sent; the `zip` above
truncates, so that is unreachable. It now states the real reason, which
is that `clippy::indexing_slicing` is denied here. The short-response
error names the document index, and the rustdoc no longer implies this
type can vouch for ordering *within* a provider's response — providers
pair embeddings to texts positionally, which is their contract, not this
builder's. That an empty `#[embed]` collection fails the whole build is
now documented rather than discovered.

* test(embeddings): make the multi-document tests able to see a borrowed run

Self-review finding. `NTexts` named every document's texts `t0..t{n-1}`,
so documents of equal length produced byte-identical text lists and a
per-document assertion of `["t0","t1","t2"]` could not tell a document's
own run from a neighbour's. Both multi-document tests claimed in their
comments to verify exactly that.

Demonstrated by mutating the reassembly to hand each document the *next*
document's run, preserving pair order and every run length. Five
pre-existing tests caught it; all five new ones passed. Texts now carry
their owner (`d{doc}t{i}`), and both multi-document tests fail under the
same mutation. The property was already covered by the older tests, so
this closes an overstated claim rather than an uncovered defect.

`OneAtATimeReversedLatency` derives its delay from the text name, so the
rename would have silently zeroed every delay and left the test asserting
correct order against a model that no longer inverts anything. It now
parses the position after the last `t` and asserts it found one.

Also, the zero-text error left the document unnamed while the error
directly beneath it — added in this PR — names one, and the rustdoc
calls that case easy to hit by accident. It now names the document and
says what caused it, which changes the message; the test that pinned the
old wording now pins the behavior plus the new message, and a second
document position is covered so the index cannot be a constant.
`build_with_usage` no longer forwards only the ordering contract, since
it is the function that actually raises both errors.

fix(rig): exclude test cassettes from the published crate (#2350)

The root manifest is the `rig` facade, so every path beside it is swept into
the published tarball. That included `tests/cassettes/`, 1,100+ provider replay
fixtures, which had grown the crate to 9.51 MiB against the crates.io 10 MiB
upload limit. That left 517 KiB of headroom on a trend that added 1.5 MiB in
the last release cycle, so the next release was on track to be rejected.

The limit is enforced server-side, so `cargo publish --dry-run` reports success
right up until the real upload fails. A 22-crate release that dies partway
through leaves the workspace half-published, and the burned versions cannot be
reused.

Excluding the cassettes takes the tarball from 9.51 MiB to 3.33 MiB, and the
file count from 1,704 to 589. They are read at runtime from
`CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR` and never embedded with `include_*!`, so nothing in the
package needs them to compile. Repo-local test runs are unaffected: `exclude`
governs packaging only, not the working tree.

fix(openrouter): surface chat-completions refusals, and map the reasoning share of usage (#2358)

* fix(openrouter): surface a chat-completions refusal instead of failing the turn

OpenRouter forwards OpenAI's structured-output refusal verbatim: a *sibling*
of `content`, never a content part.

    {"role": "assistant", "content": null,
     "refusal": "I'm sorry, I can't assist with that request."}

`NormalizeCompletionResponse` is hand-rolled here rather than routed through
the shared `normalize_openai_response`, and its destructure absorbed `refusal`
into `..`. It mapped only the *content-part* spelling, which is the Responses
API's shape and which chat completions never sends, so with `content: null`
the turn normalized to zero content and failed with the opaque
`Response contained no message or tool call (empty)`.

Two surfaces already disagreed with that on the same bytes:
`ProviderResponseExt::get_text_response` routes through
`assistant_message_text_response`, which applies the fallback, and the
streaming path uses the shared `delta_text`, which prefers a non-empty

* fix(openrouter): map the reasoning share of usage accounting

OpenRouter documents usage accounting as always included, and every
reasoning-capable route reports the breakdown -- 1,984 of 1,984 completion
tokens on a recorded `openai/o4-mini` turn, 531 of 540 on an
`anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5` one, 1,702 of 2,000 on a
`deepseek/deepseek-r1-0528` one:

    "usage": {"completion_tokens": 540,
              "completion_tokens_details": {"reasoning_tokens": 531}, ...}

`openrouter::Usage` modeled no `completion_tokens_details` field at all, so
the object was discarded at deserialization and `From<&Usage> for
completion::Usage` ended with a literal `reasoning_tokens: 0`.

rig's normalized `Usage` has a first-class `reasoning_tokens` slot that
openai, deepseek, gemini and anthropic all fill, and it is recorded onto the
`gen_ai.usage.reasoning_tokens` telemetry span -- so on OpenRouter that span,
and every caller reading the field, saw a hardcoded zero no matter what the
route billed. The same type is `OpenRouterExt::StreamingUsage`, so the
streaming terminal record reported the same zero: the two transports agreed,
which is why nothing caught it.

`openrouter::Usage` has all-public fields and no `#[non_exhaustive]`, so this
is source-level breaking for a full struct literal or an exhaustive
destructuring pattern; it derives `Default`, so `..Default::default()` and `..`
keep working, and no such shape exists in-tree.

Model the breakdown and map it. Deserialize-tolerant by construction --
absent, `null`, `{}` and unmodeled siblings (`audio_tokens`, `image_tokens`)
all read as zero -- and skipped on serialization when absent, so nothing rig
sends changes.

fix(doubleword): report the embedding width Doubleword actually returns (#2356)

* fix(doubleword): report the embedding width Doubleword actually returns

`EmbeddingModel::ndims()` did not describe the vectors Doubleword sends back,
in either direction, and both halves came from the same file.

`default_ndims` was never implemented, so `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B` — the only
embedding model the provider ships, and a public const — fell through to
OpenAI's table, matched nothing, and reported `ndims() == 0` while returning
4096-wide vectors. That number is not cosmetic: `rig-neo4j` validates an
existing vector index against it and creates a new one with it, and
`rig-sqlite` sizes its table from it, so a caller following rig's own API got a
zero-width index.

`embedding_dimensions` returned `Ok(None)` unconditionally, on the stated
grounds that the pre-migration hand-rolled request never sent the field. So a
caller-requested width was dropped on the floor:
`embedding_model_with_ndims(model, 512)` reported 512 and received 4096.
Doubleword documents the model as supporting "user-defined output dimensions
ranging from 32 to 4096", and the live API honours `dimensions` exactly —
512 returns 512, 32 returns 32.

Both are now driven by one table of documented widths, so the width the model
reports and the widths it will request cannot drift apart. Requesting the
native width sends nothing, because that is the shared path echoing back what
`default_ndims` just reported rather than a caller asking for truncation — the
same distinction Mistral draws — which also leaves every already-recorded
default-width request byte-identical.

Widths outside the documented range are refused before the request is built.
Above the ceiling Doubleword answers `200 OK` with a silently clamped 4096-wide
vector, which would have reintroduced exactly the mismatch this fixes. Below
the floor it is not dependable: the identical request answers `422
Unprocessable request` or `200` with a sub-floor vector at random — six of
fifteen live probes at 1, 2, 8, 16 and 31 dimensions were rejected, while every
probe at 32 and above succeeded. A model rig has no table for keeps the old
behaviour of sending the caller's width unvalidated.

* test(doubleword): pin the embedding-width contract with a recorded matrix

24 recorded cells under `tests/cassettes/doubleword/embedding_dimensions/`,
all asserting one invariant: the vectors Doubleword returns are exactly
`ndims()` wide. 22 of the 24 fail against `origin/main`'s `embedding.rs`, in
the two shapes the two defects predict.

The cells that ask for no width (`width_default_single`,
`usage_at_the_default_width`, `builder_documents_at_the_default_width`) send a
byte-identical request before and after the fix, so on main they fail as a
clean assertion — `4096 != 0` — with no mock miss. The cells that name a width
change what rig sends, so on main they fail as a replay miss whose diagnostic
prints both bodies side by side, plus the width mismatch behind it. That is
deliberate and is what `tests/README.md` asks for when a change intentionally
alters a request.

The matrix multiplies width (default, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4095,
explicit 4096) against input cardinality (single, batch of three, repeated),
entry point (`embed_texts`, `embed_texts_with_usage`, `EmbeddingsBuilder`) and
input class (ascii, unicode, long, empty, unserved model). Two cells are
deliberate controls that pass on main as well as after the fix:
`width_4096_single_is_not_sent` proves naming the native width still sends no
`dimensions`, and `a_zero_width_is_treated_as_no_width` pins the shared path's
rule that 0 means "the caller said nothing".

Widths outside the documented range cannot be recorded — rig now refuses them
before building a request — so they are unit-tested next to the fix instead,
along with the native-width suppression and the unknown-model passthrough.
One cell is dropped with its reason in the file: Doubleword answers a
whitespace-only input non-deterministically (400, 200, 400, 400, 200, 400 over
six consecutive live requests), so no fixture can state its premise honestly.

Each cell reads its own cassette back and asserts against the recorded bytes —
the width the response carried and the `dimensions` the request sent — through
a new registered wrapper, `with_doubleword_embedding_cassette`, so a cell whose
provider turn stopped producing the shape it is about fails instead of quietly
covering nothing.

* docs(doubleword): correct two claims the code and the vendor docs contradict

The module rustdoc told users that Doubleword's "async **and** batch tiers run
through the OpenAI-compatible Batch API (`/v1/batches`)". Only the batch tier
does. The async tier is the same realtime endpoints with
`service_tier: "flex"`, optionally plus `background: true` to poll — per
Doubleword's own async-inference page — so half the sentence pointed at the
wrong endpoint.

`response_identity_edge.rs` opened by stating that "Doubleword is an
Anthropic-compatible gateway, so it *inherits* the
`AnthropicCompatibleProvider::REQUEST_ID_HEADER` default of `request-id`".
It is bound to `OpenAICompatibleProvider` (`doubleword/client.rs`), whose
default is `None`; Anthropic's `Some("request-id")` never touches it. The
file's assertion — `provider_request_id == None` — was right, but the reason
it gave was a contract this provider does not participate in, which is exactly
what would mislead the next person deciding whether to opt in. The corrected
note keeps the real finding: both request-id spellings are on the recorder's
allowlist and neither appears in either fixture, so Doubleword demonstrably
sends none.

* fix(doubleword): correct four claims a cold review found overstated

None of these change behaviour; all four were assertions about the code or the
provider that the evidence does not support.

- The matrix's headline invariant said "every cell" holds
  `vec.len() == ndims()`. Three do not, by design: `a_zero_width_is_treated_as_no_width`

  derived "because a derived expectation would agree with whatever the code
  did" — while the helper twelve lines below derived it, on both native-width
  cells the comment singled out. Those two cells now pass `None` explicitly and
  the shared helper is restricted to truncating widths, with an assertion that
  says so.
- The changelog said any width outside 32-4096 is now rejected. Zero is outside
  it and is not rejected: the shared path reads 0 as "the caller said nothing"
  and the hook never sees it. It also said an unknown embedding model is
  "unaffected ... as before", when in fact no Doubleword model sent
  `dimensions` before, so sending it for unknown models is a real wire change
  for anyone pointing `DOUBLEWORD_BASE_URL` at a self-hosted backend. Both are

- `response_identity_edge.rs` claimed Doubleword "sends neither `request-id`
  nor `x-request-id`". It does send `x-request-id` — but only from some
  backends. Three live requests per model: `gpt-oss-20b`, `gemma-4-31B-it` and

fix(providers): survive truncated tool calls and preserve DeepSeek wire data (#2359)

* fix(providers): survive a max_tokens-truncated tool call on the blocking path

An OpenAI-compatible provider still emits the tool call when the output
budget runs out mid-arguments: the turn comes back with
finish_reason "length" and arguments cut off partway through the JSON
object. Reproduced live against deepseek-v4-flash at 24, 32, 48 and 64
token budgets -- `{"summary": `, `{"summary": "Log this incident: the`,
and so on, every one invalid -- and previously against Mistral at
24/32/48/64/96.

openai::Function, deepseek::Function and mistral::Function all parsed
that strictly, so the whole CompletionResponse failed to decode and the
turn's text, usage, id, model and finish reason went down with the
unusable call. The streaming path meanwhile keeps the turn and drops the
call (UnparseableToolInput::Drop), so the two transports disagreed about
identical wire bytes. On a parallel turn it also lost a *complete* call:
at a 56-token cap DeepSeek returns page_oncall with full arguments
beside a truncated file_report, and blocking lost both.

#2337 fixed Mistral's own copy and deferred the shared one -- "the same
strict parse exists on the shared OpenAI Function type, so every
OpenAI-compatible provider has the blocking half of this defect". This
is that change. json_utils::drop_truncated_tool_calls deserializes the
wire tool_calls array and drops only the entries whose arguments string
does not parse; the turn survives to report its Length finish reason.
Mistral's provider-local deserialize_truncatable_arguments is deleted in
favour of it.

The drop is at the array rather than on the arguments value, and that
distinction is load-bearing. Mapping a truncated payload to a sentinel
value -- Value::Null, as #2337 shipped for Mistral -- cannot work as a
shared fix: parse_tool_arguments("null") succeeds, and Groq spells a
parameterless call `"arguments": "null"`, so the sentinel is
indistinguishable from a real call. Recorded proof is already in the
tree: every zero-argument call in
tests/cassettes/groq/agent_tool_sessions/parallel_tool_calls_single_turn_nonstreaming.yaml
carries it, and a sentinel-based cut of this fix failed both of those
groq cells. Because a normalized tool call is echoed back on the next
turn, a wrong drop would also have changed what rig sends. Dropping at
the array leaves every parseable payload's semantics untouched.

The drop is deliberately narrow: only an unparseable arguments string
qualifies. Any other decode failure (a missing id, an unknown type) is a
response defect and still fails deserialization.

The blast radius is every provider whose Response is
openai::CompletionResponse -- openai, azure, groq, together,
huggingface, hyperbolic, perplexity, moonshot, minimax, llamafile,
xiaomimimo, doubleword, zai, Copilot's chat route and, by delegation,
venice -- plus openrouter, deepseek and mistral.

* fix(deepseek): lead a normalized choice with the reasoning block

NormalizeCompletionResponse built [text?, tool_call...] and then pushed
the reasoning_content block onto the end, so a reasoner turn that called
a tool normalized to [text, tool_call, reasoning]. DeepSeek's own stream
does the opposite: decoding the committed
reasoning_tool_roundtrip/streaming fixture chunk by chunk gives 27
reasoning chunks, then 12 tool-call chunks, then the finish reason. The
two transports returned differently ordered choices for the same turn.

DeepSeek was the only wire type in the tree putting reasoning last: the
shared OpenAI normalizer pushes it before the tool calls, the wire-to-rig
message conversion puts it first, and the shared canonical chunk
lifecycle fixes the order as reasoning, then text, then tool events.

No data was lost, only reordered -- but a caller rendering the choice in
order saw the model's reasoning after the action it explained. Blocking
now matches DeepSeek's own stream exactly.

* fix(deepseek): stop deleting non-text user content parts from the request

DeepSeek takes message content as a plain string, so
finalize_request_body flattens content-part arrays. It passed
only_if_all_text = false, which the shared helper documents as dropping
every non-text part -- so an attached image, audio clip, PDF or video
simply vanished, DeepSeek answered the question from the remaining text
alone, and nothing anywhere reported the loss.

Verified live that the part is not merely unsupported but explicitly
rejected: a user message carrying {"type":"image_url",...} comes back
400 "Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type:
messages[0]: unknown variant `image_url`, expected `text`". Perplexity,
the tree's other plain-text-only provider, passes true precisely so the
part survives to the wire and the API's own rejection reaches the
caller; DeepSeek was the outlier.

An all-text array still flattens to the same plain string, byte for
byte, which is why no recorded request body moved.

* test(deepseek): record the truncation, reasoning-order and wire-shape matrices

50 new cassettes across three per-bug fixture directories, each with its
own registered wrapper so the matrices stay auditable per bug.

truncation_matrix (23 cells): the max_tokens sweep 12/16/20/24/32/48/64/96
on both transports, parallel calls where only the second is cut, a turn
that spoke before it was cut, a reasoner turn cut mid-arguments, and the
agent loop on both surfaces -- plus a cross-crate decode cell over the
exact bytes the 24-token budget returned.

reasoning_block_order (10 cells): reasoner turns with one call, two
calls and text only, blocking and streaming, the non-thinking controls,
and the agent's persisted history and streamed event order. The full
blocking enumeration over every (reasoning x text x 0/1/2 calls) shape is
a unit test in providers/deepseek.rs, because the live model cannot be
made to emit a chosen shape on demand.

wire_shape_matrix (17 cells): every UserContent kind whose conversion

image-only message, the streamed twin, and the three all-text controls
that must still flatten unchanged -- plus the census cells that pin what
the hunt confirmed is *not* a bug: DeepSeek really does reject a forced
tool_choice while thinking is on (hand-built bodies, since finalization
rewrites any rig would send), the completion path preserves DeepSeek's
error envelope on a bad model and a rejected key, and the
prompt_cache_hit_tokens/miss split reaches rig's usage on both
transports.

Each cell asserts its premise against its own recorded bytes -- that the
recorded turn really did carry truncated arguments, or really did carry
none -- so a cell whose provider turn quietly changes shape fails rather
than passing while covering nothing.

chore(deps): lower dependency floors to what rig needs and stop raising them (#2195) (#2369)

* chore(deps): lower dependency floors to what rig needs and stop raising them (#2195)

A manifest requirement is a floor, not a pin — `tokio = "1"` is `^1` — but
Dependabot's default cargo strategy rewrote every floor to the latest patch on
each upstream release, and every rig release shipped those raised floors,
forcing downstream users to `cargo update` a dozen unrelated crates to take a
point release.

- Dependabot: `versioning-strategy: increase-if-necessary` — `Cargo.lock`
  moves for in-range releases; the manifest moves only for a major bump.
- Floors lowered to the lowest version rig's own code needs: a bare major
  (or `0.minor`) where rig uses only long-stable API, and the version that
  introduced a feature/API rig relies on where not (each such floor is
  annotated). The `deranged = "=0.5.8"` exact pin — a workaround for an
  upstream issue that is closed, and the one requirement that could make a
  downstream resolution *fail* — is removed. Locked versions are unchanged.
- `scripts/check-dependency-floors.py`: downgrades every direct dependency
  to its floor (bisecting to the lowest version the tree admits where a
  transitive needs more) and builds the workspace with all features and
  targets; wired into nightly.yaml as `dependency-floors`, also triggered by
  PRs touching a manifest, the lockfile, or the script.

not model, and the only global guard was `compared_pairs > 0` across the
*entire* corpus. One well-covered provider therefore kept the suite green
while another's traffic went entirely unexamined — and that was not
hypothetical: Bedrock's `/model/<id>/converse` and Ollama's `/api/chat`
were 100% unmodeled, so 72 recorded requests had never been checked by
anything.

Model both endpoints and classify every recorded request three ways
instead of two: modeled, non-conversational (embeddings, image
generation, audio, model listings — nothing with a prompt prefix to
protect), or unmodeled, meaning a conversational endpoint the table does
not know. Only the third is a finding, and it is now a finding rather
than a skip, so a future provider's chat endpoint cannot quietly opt out.
A per-provider census asserts this and prints the whole table on failure.

Both lists carry the same contract as MOVES_CACHE_PREFIX: an entry with
an empty reason is rejected, and a stale entry is reported.

The rule itself moves to tests/common/cache_prefix.rs so the per-scenario
conformance harness can apply the identical flattening rather than a
second copy that could drift apart from this one.

Coverage after the change: every one of the 18 provider directories
participates, 357 turn pairs compared (up from 342), with Bedrock and
Ollama contributing 15 pairs that were previously invisible.

* fix(gemini, cohere): serialize request-body maps in a stable order so prompt caching can hit

Two `HashMap` fields were serialized straight into request bodies:

  * `gemini::completion::Schema::properties` — a tool's JSON Schema
    argument properties, which Gemini renders in the `tools` block at the
    very *front* of the cacheable prefix;
  * `cohere::completion::Document::data` — a document's metadata and
    text, inside the `messages` block Cohere's cache keys on.

`HashMap` seeds its iteration order per instance, so both emitted their
keys in a different order on every single request. Provider prompt caches
are prefix matches over the exact request bytes, so any Gemini request
carrying a tool with two or more properties — and any Cohere request
carrying a document — had a different prefix every time and could never
hit the cache. Silently: nothing errors, the tokens are simply re-billed
in full, forever.

The fix serializes both maps in sorted key order through one shared
helper. Sorting rather than preserving insertion order matches the choice
rig already made deliberately when rendering `completion::Document`
metadata into prompt text, keeps both public field types unchanged, and
costs nothing — JSON object key order is meaningless to both APIs.

This bug class is invisible to almost every test one would think to
write, which is why it survived: cassette replay compares key-sorted
canonical JSON, and a `serde_json::Value` round-trip normalizes key order
too, so all the recorded evidence looks identical while the live wire
never repeats itself. Catching it needs the same request serialized more
than once in one process and the raw bytes compared, which is what the
new `*_request_serialization_is_deterministic` family in
tests/cassette_cache_prefix.rs does across 13 provider request builders.

On origin/main that check fails for exactly gemini and cohere and passes
for the other eleven; with this fix all thirteen pass.

* test(cache): add the cross-provider cache-conformance harness, with OpenAI and Gemini suites

Rig normalizes `Usage::cached_input_tokens` for a dozen providers, but
exactly one of them — Anthropic — had ever been *observed* caching. Every
other provider shipped cache accounting no test had seen work.

The harness (tests/common/cache_conformance.rs) runs one deterministic
three-turn probe per provider — warm, byte-identical repeat, then append
and repeat — and asserts against a per-provider `CacheSupport`
descriptor, so adding a provider is a descriptor rather than another copy
of the assertion logic. The assertion that carries the weight is
`assert_hit_ratio`: `cached_input_tokens > 0` passes happily while 39,800
of 40,000 prefix tokens go uncached, so the ratio is taken against turn
1's billed prompt, with the denominator derived per provider from its own
usage mapping and written down in `CacheAccounting` (Anthropic reports
cache tokens *alongside* `input_tokens`; everyone else reports them
*inside* it — get this backwards and the headline assertion is vacuous).

Recorded, with the measured numbers:

  * OpenAI chat completions — turn 2 read 4,480 of turn 1's 4,597 prompt
    tokens (97.5%), and turn 3 still read 4,480 after the prefix grew.
  * OpenAI Responses — same, once rig sends `prompt_cache_key`. Without
    one, turn 2 misses reproducibly while turn 3 hits; that is recorded
    as its own cell rather than hidden, because rig's turn-1 and turn-2
    request bodies are byte-identical (`assert_prefix_stable` proves it),
    so the miss is OpenAI's routing, not rig's bytes.
  * Gemini — turn 2 read 3,765 of 4,612. This is also the end-to-end
    regression cell for the `HashMap` tool-schema bug fixed in the
    previous commit: before it, Gemini could never hit at all.

Both providers get blocking, streaming and real-agent-loop cells. The
agent cells are the ones nothing else can replace: the three-turn probe
builds its own history, so it proves the *provider* caches a growing
prefix, while only a real run proves rig's agent driver does not disturb
that prefix between iterations.

Growth is asserted as a *ratio* rather than a monotonic token count.
Providers cache in coarse blocks, so the absolute figure drifts by a few
tokens as the prefix grows and block boundaries re-align — Gemini was
measured going 3,765 -> 3,760 across a 21-token append. A monotonic
assertion fails on that noise while still passing a genuine partial move;
the ratio is robust to the noise and is what determines the bill.

* test(cache): record prompt-cache suites for ten more providers, add live economics, document the doctrine

Extends the conformance harness across the rest of the matrix and, for the
first time, answers "does this provider's prompt cache actually work" with
a measured number rather than an assumption. Every provider with
credentials in this environment now has recorded evidence, and every
provider without them says why.

Measured, live (turn 2's cache read over turn 1's billed prompt):

  anthropic  99.9%   openai chat  97.5%   openai responses  97.5%
  deepseek   99.8%   openrouter   97.5%   xai               98.8%
  venice     91.2%   gemini       81.6%

Three results are worth more than the ratios:

  * **Cohere reports a constant 112 cached tokens against a 6,058-token
    prompt** — 1.8%, unchanged whether the prefix repeats or grows. It is
    non-zero, so the `cached_input_tokens > 0` assertion this harness
    replaces would have reported Cohere as "caching works" while 98% of
    every prompt was re-billed. That is precisely the silent-degradation
    case the ratio assertion exists to catch, and it is now pinned.
  * **Mistral's cache is intermittent** — the same byte-identical prefix
    hit on turn 2 in one pass, on turn 1 only in another, and not at all
    in a third, with `assert_prefix_stable` proving rig's bytes never
    moved. Its cells therefore assert the narrower thing that is true and
    deterministic: when Mistral reports a read, rig surfaces it at full
    magnitude on both paths. Claiming a hit rate would have been a coin
    flip dressed up as a test.
  * **Gemini and Mistral need a warm-up pass to record.** A cold entry
    serves only the byte-identical repeat; the grown turn-3 prefix reads
    zero until an entry for it exists. Documented in tests/README.md as a
    recording procedure, and Gemini's live cell runs two passes and
    asserts on the second.

Groq, Doubleword and Perplexity report no cached tokens at all. They get
`assert_no_meaningful_prefix_cache`, which is self-invalidating: the day
one of them ships a cache, the assertion fails and says to replace it
with the full suite. Groq's cell states its own bound — the account's
8,000 TPM tier caps the probe at ~1,800 tokens, which clears a plausible
1,024-token floor but cannot rule out a higher one.

Also here:

  * A coverage guard: a provider with cassettes and no cache scenario
    fails unless NO_CACHE_SUITE explains why. Bedrock, ChatGPT, Copilot
    and mistral.rs are unrecordable in this environment; Ollama and
    llamafile report no cached-token field at all, so there is no mapping
    to test.
  * `#[ignore]`d live economics cells for the six caching providers, each
    printing a LIVE-CACHE-ECONOMICS row so the table above can be
    regenerated rather than trusted as a transcription. All six were run.
  * The prefix rule now strips `cache_control` before comparing. Anthropic's
    documented incremental-caching pattern moves the breakpoint forward
    every turn, and comparing raw bytes reported that correct behavior as a
    violation — silently, because with the marker on the first message the
    two turns looked like unrelated conversations and the pair was skipped.
    Every multi-turn Anthropic conversation using manual prompt caching was
    invisible to the check.
  * tests/README.md gains a Prompt Cache Testing section: the four layers,
    the per-provider denominator trap, the recording rules, and an explicit
    statement of what replay does and does not prove.

* test(cache): re-record the groq and doubleword streaming fixtures after the empty-reply guard

Both were recorded before `run_cache_probe_streaming` learned to substitute a
committed placeholder for a turn-2 reply that streamed no text. Their turn-3
request bodies therefore no longer matched the recording and failed replay.
Re-recorded against the current probe.

* docs(changelog): link the cache-serialization fixes to their PR

* test(cache): fix three wrong conclusions the independent review surfaced

An independent cold review found that `assert_no_meaningful_prefix_cache`
read only the first two turns of a probe, so it could not see a cache
that warms late — and that the branch had published two wrong findings
because of it.

**Cohere does cache.** Its own committed fixture, which the previous
revision's doc contradicted: 112 of 6,058 prompt tokens on turn 1 (1.8%),
992 on a byte-identical turn 2 (16.4%), then 6,016 of 6,085 on the grown
turn 3 — 98.9%. The claim that it "reports a constant 112 cached tokens
… not prefix caching" was wrong, and because the assertion never looked
at turn 3 it would have gone on passing forever. Cohere now uses a new
`assert_cache_warms_over_turns`, pinning the two things that are true and
that a prefix move would break: the read never goes backwards as the
conversation grows, and the final turn clears the floor.

**Groq caches too**, intermittently, with Mistral's signature: its
streaming probe's first turn reads 1,792 of 1,795 (99.8%) while other
turns read zero, and repeated recordings move the hit around, with
`assert_prefix_stable` proving rig's bytes never moved. It moves to
`assert_cache_read_is_surfaced` — the same narrow, deterministic claim
Mistral makes about rig's usage mapping rather than about the provider's
hit rate.

The assertion itself now folds over **every** turn, which is what makes
its self-invalidating promise real: it caught Groq immediately on the
first run after the change. Doubleword and Perplexity still report zero
on all three turns and remain correctly classified.

Also from the review:

  * `assert_cache_read_is_surfaced`'s panic message had doubled line
    continuations, so the only diagnostic Mistral and Groq failures print
    would have contained literal backslashes and a literal `\n` instead
    of a formatted usage table.
  * `assert_warms`'s doc claimed the `reports_writes: false` branch is
    "asserted against the observation"; it is close to a tautology, since
    `cache_creation_input_tokens` is a hardcoded 0 on every one of those
    mappings. The doc now says which half of that assertion is
    load-bearing (the padding check) and which is not.
  * Removed `CacheSupport::explicit_breakpoints`, `CacheProbe::without_tools`
    and `assert_reports_no_cache` — all dead, all hidden by the module's
    `#![allow(dead_code)]`.

* test(cache): make the warming-cache assertion tolerant of block drift, and share the padding check

Follow-up findings from a focused re-review of the previous commit.

`assert_cache_warms_over_turns` asserted strict ratio monotonicity with a
1e-9 epsilon, which contradicts the doctrine the same module states two
functions earlier: providers cache in coarse blocks, so a flat cached
count against a growing prompt makes the ratio drift down by a fraction
of a percent with nothing wrong. Cohere at 6,016 cached would read
99.31% then 98.87% across a 27-token append and fail with "the cache read
went backwards" — failing on arithmetic. Today's fixture (1.8 -> 16.4 ->
98.9) has the headroom to hide that, so it was latent rather than live.

Replaced with the "once warm, stays warm" rule the agent-loop assertion
already uses: once any turn clears the provider's floor every later turn
must too, and the final turn must. A real prefix move collapses the ratio
to near zero and still trips it immediately — verified by zeroing turn
3's recorded cache read, which fails with "the final turn only reached
0.0%".

Also: `assert_cache_warms_over_turns` had no under-padding check, so
`min_cacheable_tokens` went unread for Cohere and an under-padded
re-record would have reported a low ratio rather than the real cause. The
two turn-1 sanity assertions are now a shared helper used by both it and
`assert_no_meaningful_prefix_cache`.

Two documentation corrections, both about not overstating the evidence:
the Groq module now records that its blocking fixture was re-recorded as
part of the reclassification (its previous recording read zero on every
turn and would have kept passing), and the Cohere table now names which
probe it reports and gives the streaming probe's 99.4% alongside.

* test(cache): guard every provider suite, not only those with cassettes

The cache-suite coverage guard walked `tests/cassettes`, so a provider
with no recorded fixtures at all escaped it entirely — the loudest
possible form of "nobody has ever checked whether its prompt cache
works". Eleven provider suites were in that state (azure, huggingface,
hyperbolic, llamacpp, minimax, mira, moonshot, together, voyageai,
xiaomimimo, zai).

It now walks `tests/providers`, so all 29 suites are accounted for and
each of the eleven carries an explicit reason: no credentials in this
environment, no cached-token field on the wire, or — for voyageai — not
a completion provider at all.

* test(cache): add agent-loop cells wherever the provider's model will actually use a tool

Closes the last gap against the Layer 2 matrix, which lists
`agent_multi_turn_tools` as a minimum cell. It existed only for
anthropic, openai (both surfaces) and gemini; five more providers now
have one — openrouter, venice, cohere and doubleword, joining the four
already there.

The agent cell is the only one that can catch rig's *driver* disturbing
the prefix between iterations. The three-turn probe builds its own
history, so it proves the provider caches a growing prefix; only a real
run with a tool round-trip proves the agent loop re-advertises the same
tools in the same order, rebuilds the same system prompt, and re-admits
the assistant turn unchanged. Where the provider caches reliably the cell
asserts growth; where it does not (cohere warms late, doubleword does not
cache) it asserts prefix stability alone, which is the loop-level
guarantee and holds regardless of hit rate.

Five providers get **no** agent cell, and say so in their module docs
rather than shipping a cell that cannot fail:

  * deepseek and xai answer the probe from their own knowledge and never
    call the tool, even with `ToolChoice::Required`;
  * groq and perplexity likewise;
  * mistral returns an empty response through the agent surface at the
    probe's output budget.

A run that makes one model call records one request, which leaves
`assert_prefix_stable` no pair to compare — the cell would be green
forever while proving nothing. Their loop-level coverage comes from the
corpus-wide scan instead, which compares every recorded multi-turn
conversation in their existing suites.

* test(cache): pin cache_control breakpoint placement on the wire

A line-by-line audit against the spec found `CacheSupport` was missing
`explicit_breakpoints`. An earlier commit deleted it as dead code, which
was true but was the wrong fix: the right one is to make it load-bearing,
because breakpoint placement is its own bug class and nothing in the
branch covered it.

`assert_breakpoints_match_support` reads the recorded request bodies and
asserts in both directions, so the descriptor itself is testable:

  * `explicit_breakpoints: true` — every turn must carry at least one
    `cache_control` marker, and no more than Anthropic's documented limit
    of four. A turn with none is caching silently switched off, and the
    usage counters cannot tell you that: a warm org cache still reports a
    read.
  * `explicit_breakpoints: false` — no turn may carry one. Rig sending
    `cache_control` to a provider whose API does not define it either
    errors the request or, worse, is accepted and ignored while looking
    like caching is configured.

Proven to fire by flipping the descriptor rather than tampering with a
fixture — a mutated fixture fails replay body-matching first, which would
have made the new assertion look reachable when it was not. Flipping
OpenAI to `true` fails with "turn 1 carries no `cache_control` marker";
flipping Anthropic to `false` fails with "turn 1 carries 3 markers".
Wired into the anthropic, openai, gemini, cohere and venice suites — 20
call sites.

Also documents why `CacheObservation` deliberately holds usage only and
not the outbound bodies, which the spec sketched as a `requests` field:
the cassette harness exposes no in-process copy in either mode (replay
drops the incoming bytes after matching, record mode leaves them inside
httpmock until export), so the bodies are read back from the written
fixture instead. That is the same wire bytes, works identically in both
modes, and needs no change to the cassette core; the cost is that those
assertions run after the wrapper closure rather than inside it.

feat(gemini): explicit context caching, and three usage-mapping bugs the cache audit found (#2375)

* feat(gemini): implement explicit context caching (`cachedContents`)

`crates/rig-core/src/providers/gemini/completion.rs` carried the line

    // cachedContent: Optional<String>

— a commented-out field, and the whole of rig's support for Gemini's
explicit context cache. There was no way to create the resource that
field names, and grep found zero occurrences of `cachedContents` in the
workspace.

Measured first, implemented second. On gemini-2.5-flash over one
18,497-token corpus:

  implicit  turns 1-5: 0% cached on every turn (~92k tokens billed at
                       full price); a sixth request finally read 99.6%
  explicit  turn 1:    100.0%, and 100.0% again from an unrelated
                       conversation

Explicit caching clears all three bars the evaluation set: a materially
higher ratio, a hit on the *first* request where implicit needs a
warm-up, and reuse of one corpus across conversations that share nothing
but the handle — which implicit structurally cannot do, because it keys
on a prefix a fresh conversation has not sent yet.

What ships:

  * `gemini::cached_content` — `CachedContentClient` with the full
    lifecycle (create/get/list/update-expiry/delete), `NewCachedContent`
    builder, and `CacheExpiry` as an enum so `ttl` and `expireTime`
    cannot both be set (Gemini rejects a body carrying both).
  * `CachedContentError::Expired`, separated from the other failures
    because it is the one a caller handles rather than propagates —
    Gemini answers a lapsed handle with 403 or 404 depending on how long
    ago it lapsed, and callers should not have to match on that.
  * The typed `cachedContent` request field, `CompletionModel::
    with_cached_content`, and `GenerateContentRequest::with_cached_content`,
    which rejects the conflicts Gemini rejects — a cache owns the system
    instruction, tools and tool choice, and the provider's own 400 does
    not say which of the three you set.
  * `Client::patch`/`Client::delete`, which no rig provider had needed
    before; a resource with a lifecycle does.

Recorded live: `explicit_cache_lifecycle` (create → get → list → update
→ delete), `explicit_cache_hit_ratio` (99.3-99.7% from turn one against a
0.95 floor, versus implicit's 0.75), and
`explicit_cache_across_conversations`.

Cache handles are server-generated and account-scoped, and they ride in
request bodies, request *paths* and responses alike. The generated-token
scrubber could not reach them — it consumes `is_token_char`, which
excludes `/`, so a `cachedContents/` prefix stopped the token at the
slash — so the cassette scrubber grew `scrub_resource_names`, with tests
pinning that the same handle maps to the same placeholder everywhere it
appears and that the bare collection path survives untouched.

* fix(gemini): stop dropping thinking, cached and tool-use tokens on the Interactions surface

`InteractionUsage` had three fields — `total_input_tokens`,
`total_output_tokens`, `total_tokens` — while Gemini's Interactions wire
reports six. The other three went on the floor:

  * `total_thought_tokens` — routinely the *largest* component. A
    cassette recorded months ago reports `input=14, output=34,
    total=270`, of which 222 tokens are thinking. Rig normalized that to
    `reasoning_tokens: 0` and a triple whose parts sum to 48 against a
    reported total of 270.
  * `total_cached_tokens` — so `Usage::cached_input_tokens` was
    structurally zero on this surface no matter what Gemini said. Any
    caller measuring cache effectiveness through the Interactions API was
    reading a hardcoded zero.
  * `total_tool_use_tokens` — rig has a field for it and used it on the
    generateContent surface but not this one.

The total fallback also summed only input and output. On this surface
thinking and tool-use tokens are reported *beside* that pair rather than
inside it, so a response that omitted `total_tokens` understated it by
the whole thinking spend; the fallback now counts every component.

No new recording was needed to find or prove this — the evidence was
already in the committed corpus.
`interactions_usage_surfaces_thinking_and_cached_tokens` replays
`interactions_api/basic_interaction_returns_id` and fails on origin/main
with `reasoning_tokens: 0`, alongside five unit tests covering each
field, the total fallback, and a wire that omits the new fields (so an
older recording keeps replaying).

* fix(vertexai): stop discarding Vertex's thinking-token count

Same bug class as the Gemini Interactions surface, found by the same
audit. `crates/rig-vertexai/src/types/completion_response.rs` mapped
Vertex usage with `reasoning_tokens: 0` hardcoded, while the SDK type it
reads from (`google-cloud-aiplatform-v1`'s `UsageMetadata`) exposes
`thoughts_token_count: i32`. Every Vertex response silently dropped its
thinking spend, which on the sibling Gemini surface is routinely the
largest component of the bill.

The other half of that finding turned out to be a non-issue and is worth
recording as such: the non-`Option` `cached_content_token_count as u64`
cast looked like a deserialization hazard next to gemini-core's
`.unwrap_or_default()`, but the generated SDK type is non-`Option` with a
default, so an omitted field decodes as 0 rather than failing. No fix
needed there.

Also pins that Gemini's `cacheTokensDetails` is *correctly* absent from
the normalized `Usage`. It is populated on the wire
(`[{"modality":"TEXT","tokenCount":3660}]`) and rig has no modality
concept to map it onto, but it survives on `GenerateContentResponse` via
`raw_completion` — the documented escape hatch. The new cell asserts that
path stays open and that the breakdown always sums to the aggregate rig
does normalize, so the two cannot silently disagree.

* test(gemini): pin the threshold edge and two prefix mutations, and document the doctrine

Three cells that say what the hit-ratio assertions cannot:

  * `below_minimum_does_not_cache` — a ~300-token prefix, deliberately
    under Gemini's documented 1,024-token floor, must read zero. This is
    the cell that gives every *other* cell's padding its meaning: if
    Gemini cached a prefix this small, the floor in GEMINI_CACHE_SUPPORT
    would be superstition and none of the padding would be proving
    anything. It asserts its own premise too, failing if the probe drifts
    above the minimum.
  * `changing_the_system_instruction_misses` — one word changed at the
    front of the prefix must cost the cache. Every other cell proves
    caching happens; this proves it is keyed on what it claims to be
    keyed on. A "hit" here would mean serving a prefix the caller never
    sent.
  * `changing_temperature_still_hits` — asserted as a hit, because
    per-request sampling changes are routine and a cache that broke on
    them would deserve a warning in rig's docs. It does not break.

tests/README.md gains a Gemini section contrasting the two caching
features with the measured numbers, plus the operational rules this work
paid for: run implicit scenarios twice, disable thinking, delete the
caches you create, and never assert a literal handle.

* docs(changelog): link the gemini cache entries to their PR

* docs(gemini): fix the cached-content intra-doc link and doctest imports

CI caught two things I did not: `GenerateContentRequest` lives in
`completion::gemini_api_types`, not `completion`, so the intra-doc link
was unresolved under `-D rustdoc::broken-intra-doc-links`; and the
module example called `completion_model` without `CompletionClient` in

Both are checks the verification list already names — `cargo doc
--workspace --no-deps` and the doctests — and I ran neither locally

* test(gemini): cover CachedContentError::Expired, and correct a token count

`Expired` was argued for in the design — it is the one failure a caller
handles rather than propagates, so a lapsed cache is recreated instead of
reported — and then shipped with zero tests. That is the shape of thing
that is quietly broken.

Deleting a cache reaches the same state as a lapsed TTL without waiting
for one. The recorded fixture shows what makes the variant worth having:
Gemini answers a deleted handle with **403**, which a caller reading raw
status codes would reasonably take for a permission problem rather than
"this cache is gone". The cell also asserts the message names the handle,
since a run juggling several caches needs to know which one lapsed.

Also corrects `below_minimum_does_not_cache`'s stated size: the probe
bills 205 prompt tokens, not the ~300 claimed in the doc comment and the
PR body. Still well under the 1,024 floor, so the cell's premise holds —
but the number was wrong and the cell asserts its own premise anyway.

* fix(gemini): refuse a cached-content handle smuggled through additional_params, and fix what the review found

An independent cold review returned "no, I would not merge this as-is",
with two of the tests written to guard this change guarding nothing.

**A real wire bug (major).** `additional_params` is `#[serde(flatten)]`,
and serde emits flattened fields *after* the named ones — so a
`cachedContent` in there overwrote the typed field. Reproduced:

    with_cached_content("cachedContents/typed")  -> Ok
    wire body                                    -> "cachedContents/SMUGGLED"

The caller silently sent a different handle than they asked for, and the
conflict validation (system instruction / tools / tool choice) was
bypassed entirely, because it only inspects the typed fields. Setting the
handle both ways is now refused, naming the smuggled value. The test that
was supposed to catch this asserted the *opposite* precedence while
passing an unrelated key (`topK`), so it never exercised the collision.

**A test that did not call the code it tested (major).** The vertexai
test built a `UsageMetadata` and then re-implemented the mapping inline
in its own body, so reverting the production fix left it green. It now
drives `CompletionResponse::try_from`, and reverting the fix fails it
with `left: 0, right: 222`.

**Unencoded pagination cursor (major).** `list()` concatenated the page
token into the query string raw, thirty lines from a sibling
(`model_listing.rs`) that routes through `with_query_pairs` and has a
test pinning `pageToken=weird+token%26x%3D1`. A `+`, `&`, `=` or `/` in a
cursor would truncate it or inject a parameter, silently dropping pages.
Now uses the same helper.

**Public fields defeated the `CacheExpiry` enum (minor).** The type's own
doc claimed both-set was unrepresentable while
`NewCachedContent { ttl: Some(..), expire_time: Some(..), .. }` compiled.
Fields are private now, reachable only through the builder — which also
lets `tools()`/`tool_config()` hold typed values and go back to returning
`Self` instead of `Result`, so two of nine builder methods no longer
break the chain for an implementation detail.

**403 discarded the provider's message (minor).** A 403 also covers a
disabled key, a project without the API enabled, and quota denial;
collapsing those into "expired" while dropping the body threw away the
only text saying which. `Expired` now carries the message.

**A dead scrubber guard (minor).** `token_end` accepts offset 0
unconditionally, so a non-token character right after `cachedContents/`
came back as the "id" — `cachedContents/"` swallowed the closing quote
and would write invalid JSON into a fixture. The id must now be entirely
token characters, with tests for the empty-handle and prose cases.

Also merges two `### Fixed` headings that landed in one `[Unreleased]`
block.

* test(gemini): exhaustive cachedContents create matrix — 108 recorded cells, plus the free validation matrix

Three tiers, split by what each costs.

**Free, exhaustive (no socket, no fixture).** The client-side surface is
where the full Cartesian product is affordable, so it is taken:

  * all 2^3 combinations of the fields a cached content owns
    (system instruction / tools / tool choice) against a handle, asserting
    the clean combination is accepted and each of the other seven is
    refused *naming every conflict* — which is the whole advantage over
    the provider's own 400, since Gemini's does not say which you set;
  * 8 handle-syntax shapes, 5 model-qualification spellings, 4
    resource-path forms, 6 TTL encodings, 5 expiry orderings, and the
    empty-cache rejection.

**Recorded, exhaustive (108 cells).** Every combination of payload
(system instruction / contents / both) x tools (none / one / three) x
tool choice (absent / auto) x display name (absent / present) x expiry
(relative TTL / absolute timestamp / provider default). Each cell creates
a cache just over the 1,024-token minimum and deletes it, so the whole
matrix recorded in 71 seconds and left **zero** live caches behind — the
delete runs on the failure path too, which matters at this size because
storage bills until it lands.

Every cell asserts the same four invariants (handle shape, model binding,
stored tokens against the minimum, expiry returned), so a provider change
to any of them fails across all 108 rather than in one hand-picked
scenario.

The dimensions and their assertions were measured live first, not
assumed:

  * the create minimum is 1,024 tokens — 720 is rejected citing
    `min_total_token_count`, 1,080 is accepted;
  * `ttl` + `expireTime` together is a 400 reading "oneof field
    'expiration'", which is direct evidence for `CacheExpiry` being an
    enum rather than two Options;
  * omitting both defaults to one hour;
  * a `toolConfig` with no `tools` is accepted;
  * an unqualified model id is a 400, which is why `NewCachedContent::new`
    qualifies it.

108 fixtures, 10.4 KB average, 1.3 MB total; all replay key-free in 1.3s
and none contains an API key, project id, or unscrubbed handle.

* test(gemini): add the cachedContents edge cells, and make list() pagination actually testable

Seven cells the create matrix cannot reach, each pinning behaviour
measured live rather than assumed:

  * a cache under the 1,024-token minimum is refused, citing
    `min_total_token_count` — the cell that proves the number the whole
    matrix pads against is real;
  * an `expireTime` **in the past is accepted**, creating a cache that is
    dead on arrival and still bills for storage. Surprising enough to pin
    precisely because it is; rig cannot prevent it without a clock, and
    guessing the caller's intent would be worse;
  * omitting both expiry forms defaults to one hour;
  * deleting a handle twice reports the second as `Expired` rather than
    silently succeeding;
  * `update_expiry` with an absolute timestamp uses the `expireTime`
    update mask, not the `ttl` one;
  * streaming against a handle reads the prefix from cache — the cache
    counters arrive on a different frame when streaming and the
    accumulator has to carry them, a bug class that has bitten this
    provider family before.

**`list()` pagination was untestable, and the first attempt at testing it
proved nothing.** With the page size hardcoded to 1,000, three caches
came back in a single page with no cursor — the loop and its
cursor-does-not-advance guard never ran, exactly the gap the review
flagged. Proving it otherwise would mean creating a thousand billed
caches.

`list_with_page_size` fixes that, and is defensible on its own terms (a
caller holding thousands of caches may want smaller responses). With a
page size of 1 and three caches the recorded fixture now shows three GETs
following two real cursors and terminating on the third — the loop is
exercised rather than trusted. Worth noting the cursors are base64url, so
the unencoded-cursor bug fixed earlier was latent rather than live; the
encoded path is now the one under test.

115 cachedContents fixtures in total, all replaying key-free, and the
account holds zero live caches after the full record — every cell deletes
what it created, including on the failure path.

* fix(gemini): validate cached-content handles at the wire, scrub pagination cursors, and cut the matrix to what it proves

Second cold review returned "no" again, and was right again.

**The major finding was only half fixed.** The smuggling guard was
attached to `with_cached_content`, so the plainest external route — put
`cachedContent` in `additional_params` and never touch the typed API —
still reached the wire with *all* conflict validation skipped.
Reproduced: a handle alongside a `systemInstruction`, built without
complaint. The check now runs where the request is built: the handle is
lifted out of `additional_params` into the typed field and validated
there, so every route reaches it. Setting it twice with different values
is refused as ambiguous; the same value twice is fine. Five tests cover
the routes.

**Real cache ids were leaking inside pagination cursors.** Gemini's
`cachedContents` cursors are base64 protobuf carrying the resource ids of
the entries either side of the page boundary, so a recorded cursor
re-exposed two ids that were placeholdered everywhere else in the same
fixture. My own audit missed it — I decoded base64 looking for API keys
and project ids, not for the ids the fixture had just redacted.

Cursors are now placeholdered rather than blanket-redacted, because
distinct cursors must stay distinct: the loop that follows them compares
each against the last to spot a server that stops advancing, and
collapsing them would end that loop early on replay. The scrub is
idempotent, which the cassette safety check enforces by re-scrubbing its
own output.

**The 108-cell create matrix is now 8 cells and a serialization test.**
Recording all 108 is what revealed the problem: Gemini's create response
never echoes `tools` or `toolConfig`, so a cell could not tell whether
the tools it asked for were sent at all — the cache could discard them
entirely and all 72 tool-bearing fixtures would still pass. What they
actually pinned was the request body, through the cassette matcher.

So the request body is pinned directly instead, across all 108
combinations, for free — and that test *does* assert the tool count,
proven by dropping the tools and watching it fail where the fixtures did
not. Eight recorded cells keep one arm of each dimension under test for
provider acceptance. 164 KB instead of 1.3 MB, for strictly more
coverage.

Also: the edge cells now delete before they assert (they leaked a billed
cache on a failed assertion, contradicting this module's own doc);
`Expired`'s message is asserted rather than merely carried — Google's own
403 text conflates "not found" and "permission denied", which is why it
has to survive; and `NewCachedContent`'s dropped `Clone` now carries its
rationale, since what callers share is the returned handle, not the
request that made it.

fix(gemini): six cachedContents defects the follow-up audit found (#2379)

* fix(gemini): triage cachedContents failures by status, and refuse a handle that retargets the request path

Two defects in the resource client that shipped in #2375, both invisible
to the recorded cassettes because both need a transport or a caller the
fixtures never exercise.

**`Expired` was unreachable outside the bundled transports.** `send_json`
matched one error variant, `InvalidStatusCodeWithDetails`. `H` is a
public extension point (`ClientBuilder::http_client`), and a custom
`HttpClientExt` may report the same 404 as a bare `InvalidStatusCode` or
as `InvalidStatusCodeWithMessage` — both fell through to the catch-all
`Http(error)` arm. Worse, a transport that hands a non-success response
back as `Ok` rather than as an error (rig's own test double does exactly
that) sent the *error body* into `serde_json::from_str::<CachedContent>`,
so a 404 surfaced as `Serde("missing field \`name\`")` — a deserialization
failure standing in for a status. Either way the recovery this module
documents — match `Expired`, recreate the cache — silently never fired
for anyone not on the bundled reqwest clients.

Triage now runs on the *status* (`error.non_success_status()`), with an
`Ok(non-success)` arm of the kind `client::Client::verify` and
`internal::model_listing::decode_json_response` already carry, and a
shared `classify_failure` so the two paths cannot drift apart. A failed
body read no longer cancels the triage either: the status is already in
hand, and dropping to `Http` there would discard the one thing that says
the handle is gone.

`InvalidStatusCode` carries no body and a non-success response may have
an empty one, so `NO_RESPONSE_BODY` stands in — an empty message left
both `CachedContentError` Displays ending in a bare colon, which reads as
truncated output rather than as a provider that said nothing.

**A handle spliced into the request path could retarget the call.**
`resource_path` interpolated whatever it was given. This is not the
malformed-URL-the-provider-rejects case it looks like:
`GeminiExt::build_uri` switches its key separator to `&` the moment it
sees a `?` in the path, so `delete("abc?stale")` issues a perfectly
well-formed `DELETE /v1beta/cachedContents/abc?stale&key=…` and destroys
the cache named `abc`. A `#` truncates the path the same way, a `/`
retargets it at another resource, and an empty id aims the request at the
*collection*. `update_expiry` was worse still — its `?updateMask=` would
land inside the caller's query string.

Refusing beats percent-encoding: the id is server-assigned and opaque, so
a caller holding one that needs escaping is holding a bug, and encoding
would have to escape the id while leaving the optional `cachedContents/`
prefix intact — two rules for one string, in service of quietly rewriting
input that is always wrong. `.` is excluded from the accepted set so a
`..` segment cannot traverse; `-` and `_` are admitted because the
cassette scrubber rewrites recorded ids to `cached-REDACTED_1` and a
replayed cell hands that straight back to `delete`.

Six status-triage cells cover each transport shape, the 403-on-`create`
asymmetry (no handle exists yet, so reporting `Expired` would send a
caller into a recreate loop), and the empty-body Display. The
mis-targeting cell drives `get`, `delete` and `update_expiry` through
four hostile handles and asserts nothing reaches the socket at all.

* fix(gemini): bound the cachedContents listing loop, and report when it was truncated

`list_with_page_size` looped on `loop {}`. A cursor that keeps *changing*
without making progress — a gateway alternating between two values, or
one minting a fresh cursor per request — defeats the
cursor-does-not-advance guard, which only remembers the previous cursor,
so `list` never returns while `all` grows without bound. That is rig#2334
again, on a resource that could not reuse the helper which already fixed
it: `internal::model_listing::paginate_models` is typed on
`Model`/`ModelListingError` and fetches through `get_bytes`, which
collapses the 403/404 triage `CachedContentError::Expired` exists for.

So the three termination rules are restated here against the same
`MAX_LISTING_PAGES` bound, and a restated rule is a rule that can drift —
which is what the tests are for.

Both non-terminating cases now say so, because nothing else can tell the
caller: whether rig stopped because Gemini ended the listing or because
rig ran out of pages, the caller gets the same `Vec<CachedContent>` and
the same `Ok`. An operator silently handed the first thousand pages of
their caches has no way to know the rest exist.

The ceiling is tracked with a flag set by the loop rather than inferred
from `page_token`, and rig#2339 is why: the loop breaks while still
holding the *previous* page's cursor, so a `page_token.is_some()` test
reports a truncation on every listing that fetched more than one page.
`a_completed_multi_page_listing_reports_no_page_ceiling` is the cell that
fails if anyone reaches for that shortcut again.

Five unit cells cover what is visible in the returned `Vec` — absent,
empty, repeated and alternating cursors, plus the percent-encoded cursor
— and `gemini_cached_content_listing_warnings.rs` covers what is not:
that a completed multi-page listing warns about nothing, that an ordinary
single-page listing is silent, that a genuinely exhausted budget still
reports the ceiling, and that a repeated cursor reports itself alone
rather than also claiming a ceiling. It is the `model_listing_warnings.rs`
pattern, for the same reason and against the same regression.

The malformed-cursor cells are the ones a recording cannot reach: no live
response carries an empty, repeated or alternating cursor. The ordinary
paths stay recorded — `prompt_caching/explicit_cache_lifecycle` for a
single page, `cached_content_matrix/edge_list_pagination` for three pages
at `pageSize=1`.

* docs(gemini): say what can actually read from a cached content, and make the tools conflict say it too

`with_cached_content` documented the constraint as "the cache owns the
system instruction and tool set, so don't send your own", and the
conflict error offered one remedy: *move them into the cache*. That is
exactly right for a system instruction — it is the feature — and wrong
for tools, in a way a caller only discovers after paying to create a
cache nothing can use.

The reason is structural rather than a gap rig could close. An `Agent`
derives the declarations it sends and the handles it dispatches through
from a single tool-registry snapshot, so it can only ever dispatch a tool
it advertised, and a call to a tool it never advertised is an invalid
tool call rather than a dispatch. Function declarations that live in the
cache are therefore declarations an agent can never execute. The converse
is representable and rig uses it — `OutputMode::Tool` advertises a
synthetic output tool that is deliberately not executable — but that only
ever adds declarations, never dispatch reach.

Follow the bare remedy and you get a cache holding a tool set, an agent
that must advertise nothing to use it, and no way to run the tools in
between. The tools arm of the conflict now says so, and names
`CompletionModel` as the surface that can: drive it yourself and run the
loop by hand.

Gated on *function* declarations rather than on the field being present,
because a provider-hosted tool is the exception that makes the rule worth
stating precisely: `codeExecution` runs on Gemini's side and needs no
loop, so a cache carrying one is usable from an agent that declares
nothing itself, and telling that caller to go write a tool loop would be
nonsense.

The docs now enumerate what an agent can actually bring to a cache, since
"no preamble, no tools, no tool choice" has non-obvious corners: native
structured output is fine (the schema rides in `generationConfig`, and
the default `OutputMode::Auto` resolves there for a tool-less agent);
`OutputMode::Tool` is not, and `Extractor` pins it, so extractors cannot
read from a cache at all; `Prompted` is not either, because it writes the
schema into the preamble; context documents are fine, being chat history
rather than system instruction; and a configured tool choice is sent even
by a tool-less agent, so it has to go too.

**The conflict matrix was asserting nothing about tools.** The sentence
after the conflict clause names all three fields unconditionally ("already
owns the system instruction, tools and tool choice"), so
`message.contains("tools")` was true for every cell in the matrix,
including the ones that set no tools at all. It now splits the clause off
and asserts the tool set is named *exactly when* it conflicted — which is
the whole advantage over the provider's own 400.

`an_agent_with_tools_cannot_read_from_a_cache` pins the finding from the
outside: the rig-core unit tests can build a request without tools,
whereas an agent holding a tool has no way not to send it. And
`deleting_twice` now asserts the `Expired` message says which failure it
was, rather than merely being non-empty.

* test(gemini): delete the cache even when the assertion fails

Every recorded `cachedContents` cell creates a cache, asserts something
about it, and deletes it — and Gemini bills storage per token-hour from
the moment `create` returns until the delete lands. An assertion that
takes the cell down between the two leaks a billed cache until its TTL
lapses. That only costs money under `RIG_PROVIDER_TEST_MODE=record`,
which is precisely when a newly written assertion is most likely to be
the one that fails.

Some cells already handled this by hand, computing a failure into an
`Option<String>`, deleting, then panicking on it. That works, and it does
not scale: it only covers the assertions this suite writes itself.
`run_cache_probe` and `assert_cache_conformance`
(`tests/common/cache_conformance.rs`) are shared by every provider's
cache suite and panic from the inside, as does every `.expect()` on an
intermediate `get`/`list`/`update_expiry` — so the lifecycle, hit-ratio,
cross-conversation, streaming and pagination cells all had windows the
hand-rolled pattern could not close.

`always_deleting_cached_contents` catches the unwind instead, and the
asymmetry in what it does with a delete failure is the point:

  * body panicked — the body's panic wins, because a cleanup that also
    failed must never overwrite the assertion actually under test. The
    handles still get named on stderr, which libtest prints under the
    failing test, which is exactly when someone needs them.
  * body passed — a delete that failed *is* the leak this exists to
    prevent, so it fails the cell.

Every handle is attempted regardless of the ones before it failing: the
pagination cell holds three caches, and an early 500 that aborted the
loop would leak two of them — the same bug as no cleanup at all, for two
thirds of the cost.

Four cells cover the guard, one of which decides the asymmetry: a body
that panicked *and* a cleanup that failed. Neither of the obvious two can
see the ordering — the panicking-body case stubs `OK`, so there is no
cleanup failure to lose to, and the 500 cases pass a body that never
panics. Swap the `resume_unwind` and the `failures` assert and all three
stay green while the assertion under test is replaced by the delete's
500. That is exactly what a failed recording run looks like: the new
assertion fails, and the delete behind it answers 403 because the cache
is already gone.

A local axum stub rather than a cassette, because the behaviour under
test is the failure path and a fixture only ever records a passing run.

`edge_list_pagination` also stops unwrapping its creates: a second cache
that failed to create still has to delete the first, or the failure leaks
three times the storage a passing run does. And `edge_below_minimum`
deletes the cache it did not expect to get, so the day Gemini lowers the
floor that cell fails having cleaned up rather than leaking out of an
`expect_err`.
