* docs(changelog): record the two cachedContents fixes

* fix(gemini): lift systemInstruction and toolConfig out of additional_params

`additional_params` is `#[serde(flatten)]` and serde emits flattened
entries *after* the named fields, so anything a caller puts there wins on
the wire while the typed field — the one every validation in this module
inspects — stays empty. `cachedContent` was lifted out for exactly that
reason. The other two fields a cached content owns were not, and they had
the same two problems.

**They walked past the cached-content conflict check.** That check reads
`self.system_instruction` / `self.tools` / `self.tool_config`; a
`systemInstruction` or `toolConfig` sitting in the flattened blob is none
of those. So a request carrying a cache handle *and* a smuggled system
instruction was accepted, dispatched, and answered by Gemini with the
400 the check exists to pre-empt — while the docs added alongside it
promised "rig rejects that before the request goes out rather than
letting Gemini answer 400". Reproduced against a capture server: the body
left the process carrying `cachedContent` and both smuggled keys.

**They were serialized twice, cache or no cache.** Neither field carries
`skip_serializing_if`, so a request using either emitted the key once as
the typed `null` and once from the blob. Every such request has been
sending duplicate JSON keys and relying on the receiver taking the last
one.

Both now come out of the blob and into the typed field, through one
`take_typed_from_additional_params` helper so a third field added later
has an obvious place to go. Deserializing rather than moving the raw
`Value` is part of the point: a malformed field is reported here, naming
itself, instead of as a provider 400 quoting a JSON path.

Setting one field both ways is now refused rather than resolved by
serialization order. A preamble and an `additional_params.systemInstruction`
are two answers to one question, and the old behaviour — silently discard
the preamble the caller wrote — is not a defensible way to pick. This
matches how a doubly-set `cachedContent` is already treated.

Four cells cover it, each verified by mutation: reverting the lift fails
all four, and none of them passes for the shape it does not test.

* docs+test(gemini): the two cache claims that had nothing checking them

Both were asserted in prose by the docs that landed earlier in this
branch, and neither had a test. One of them was wrong.

**"An agent holding a tool has no way not to send it" is false.** An
empty `RequestPatch::active_tools` allow-list empties the tool snapshot
for a turn, so a tool-holding agent builds a request with no `tools` and
the handle is accepted. That is a supported, tested configuration in
rig-agent, not a loophole — the docs simply overstated the constraint
into an absolute. `edge_agent_active_tools_suppressed` records it end to
end, so the exception is a recording rather than a claim, and the
neighbouring "an agent with tools is refused" cell no longer reads as
covering a case it does not.

What the correction does not change is the conclusion: suppressing the
tools buys the *request*, never the dispatch. The agent's own tools are
gone for that turn and the cache's were never reachable, so "move them
into the cache" is still the wrong remedy.

**The `codeExecution` carve-out was untested in both directions.** The
tools caveat is gated on the request declaring *functions* rather than on
`tools` being present, because a provider-hosted tool runs on Gemini's
side and needs no loop — telling that caller to go write one would be
nonsense. Nothing checked the gate: replacing it with `self.tools.is_some()`
left all 1,522 rig-core unit tests and the whole gemini binary green,
while handing a `codeExecution` caller a paragraph about dispatching
declarations they never wrote.

Now covered from both ends. Three shapes that must *not* earn the caveat
(`codeExecution`, `googleSearch`, an empty `functionDeclarations` list)
and one that must, all through `additional_params.tools` — the route that
actually carries provider-hosted tools. The mutation above now fails.

And because the gate encodes a claim about the provider, not just about
rig, `edge_cached_code_execution` measures it: a cache carrying only
`codeExecution`, used by an agent that declares nothing itself, runs the
tool on Gemini's side and returns the product. That is the sentence in
the docs — "a cache carrying one is usable from an agent that declares
nothing itself" — with a recording behind it.

Both cassettes replay key-free, and the account holds zero live caches
after recording: each cell deletes what it created, including on the
failure path.

* test(gemini): make the discarded leak warning observable

`always_deleting_cached_contents` warns on exactly one path: the body
panicked *and* the cleanup delete failed. On that path the body's panic
is re-raised, which is the right call — but it means the warning leaves
no trace the test can see, so from the outside the guard is
indistinguishable from one that never warned.

Mutation-verified: deleting the whole `eprintln!` block left all four
cells green. With that regression, a recording run whose new assertion
fails and whose cleanup then 500s prints the assertion and nothing else
— and the handle of a cache that is still billing is never named
anywhere, which is precisely the outcome the block's own doc comment says
it exists to prevent.

The warning now goes through a reporter the internal
`always_deleting_cached_contents_reporting` takes, defaulting to
`eprintln!` for real cells (libtest prints captured stderr under the
failing test, which is when someone needs it) and collected into a `Vec`
by the two cells that assert on it: one that the warning fires and names
the handle, and one that a *successful* cleanup after a panicking body
stays silent, so nobody is sent hunting for a cache that is already gone.

* docs(changelog): record the additional_params lifting fix

* test(gemini): assert the two new cassette cells against what was actually sent and returned

Both cells asserted only the model's answer, which is the one thing that
proves neither claim.

`a_cache_carrying_a_provider_hosted_tool_is_usable_from_an_agent` checked
that the reply contained `54173879`. A model can multiply two five-digit
numbers in its head and return exactly that with no tool involved, so the
cell would have passed just as well against a Gemini that ignored the
cached `codeExecution` entirely — which is precisely the thing it exists
to rule out. The recording does prove it, and now the test reads it:
`executableCode` carrying `print(7919 * 6841)` and `codeExecutionResult`
carrying `OUTCOME_OK` with the product, i.e. Python generated and run on
Gemini's side.

`an_agent_that_suppresses_its_tools_may_read_from_a_cache` checked that
the reply said "suppressed". Its whole claim is about what *left the
process* — a `tools` field suppressed by the allow-list, a handle sent
alongside — and a passing prompt says nothing about either.

`assert_recorded_requests_read_from_a_cache` states that shared premise
once: every recorded `generateContent` carries a `cachedContents/` handle
and none of the three fields the cache owns. Verified by pointing it at
`prompt_caching/temperature_change_still_hits`, an implicit-caching
scenario with no handle, where it fails on both counts.

`recorded_request_bodies` is `recorded_request_generation_configs`
generalized — the latter now calls it — and skips bodyless interactions,
because a `cachedContents` scenario records its own `GET` and `DELETE`
beside the completion and those carry no body.

* fix(gemini): detect smuggled cache-owned fields instead of parsing them

The previous commit made the cached-content conflict check see
`systemInstruction` and `toolConfig` set through `additional_params` by
deserializing them into rig's own types. A second review found that the
cure was worse than the disease, three times over, and it was right.

**`allowedFunctionNames` was silently dropped.** rig's
`FunctionCallingMode` spells the field `allowed_function_names`, and its
`rename_all = "UPPERCASE"` renames the *variants*, not their fields — so
the `allowedFunctionNames` Gemini's REST API actually uses never matched.
A caller sending

    {"toolConfig":{"functionCallingConfig":
      {"mode":"ANY","allowedFunctionNames":["get_weather"]}}}

got `{"mode":"ANY"}` on the wire: a request restricted to one function
became a request free to call any function, with no error anywhere. That
is worse than the bypass it was fixing.

**Modes rig does not model became hard errors.** `MODE_UNSPECIFIED` is
the proto default and `VALIDATED` was added after rig's enum was written;
both stopped building at all, and so would whatever Google adds next.

**`Content` is narrower than the wire too** — a closed `Role`, only the
lowerCamelCase part spellings — so system instructions Gemini accepts no
longer built either.

The common error is treating `additional_params` as something to parse.
It is the escape hatch for wire shapes rig has no type for; narrowing it
through a type is the one thing this path must never do. So nothing is
lifted or parsed now: `smuggled_field` reports only *which spelling* a
key appeared under, the value is left exactly where the caller put it,
and the conflict check in `with_cached_content` reads `additional_params`
alongside the typed fields — which also means it now covers a caller who
builds the request themselves, not just `create_request_body`.

Both proto-JSON spellings are checked. Gemini accepts a field under its
lowerCamelCase alias *and* its original proto name, so a check that knew
only `toolConfig` documented `tool_config` as its own bypass.

`a_smuggled_field_reaches_the_wire_exactly_as_the_caller_wrote_it` is the
cell that forbids the reverted implementation: five shapes rig has no
type for, asserted byte-identical on the wire. Re-introducing the typed
round-trip fails it, and removing `additional_params` from the guard
fails the two conflict cells.

Also: an explicit `null` counts as unset rather than as a value the
caller set; and `assert_recorded_requests_read_from_a_cache` identifies
completions by the absence of a top-level `model` rather than the
presence of `contents`, since a cache created with `content(..)` carries
`contents` too and was being held to a rule about handles it is in the
middle of minting.

* fix(gemini): validate every spelling of the cached-content handle, and correct what the set-twice errors claim

A third review, and the previous commit's own argument turned back on it.

**The handle itself knew one spelling.** That commit added
`SYSTEM_INSTRUCTION`/`TOOL_CONFIG` spelling pairs on the grounds that
"a check that knew only `toolConfig` documented `tool_config` as its own
bypass" — three lines above a `cachedContent` lift matching a single
literal. `cached_content` is a working wire spelling; measured against
the live API, it reaches the cache lookup and answers `CachedContent not
found` for a bogus handle. A handle written that way was never lifted, so
`with_cached_content` was never called and every check it owns was
skipped — the conflict refusal, the `cachedContents/<id>` shape check,
the string-type check, the set-twice comparison — while the handle sailed
onto the wire through the flattened blob. Both spellings are lifted now,
each fed through `with_cached_content`, so two spellings naming different
caches meet the set-twice rule already there.

**`tools` was read only from the typed field.** The comment justified
that by saying `extract_tools_from_additional_params` has already run —
true via `create_request_body`, and `with_cached_content` is `pub`. On a
hand-built request the blob is where the tools live, so declarations sat
beside a handle in one body with nothing refusing them, which is the
shape the check exists for. The blob is read for `tools` too now, and the
function-declaration scan that gates the tools caveat reads both
`functionDeclarations` and `function_declarations`.

**Both set-twice messages described provider behaviour that does not
happen.** They said the wire carries both copies and Gemini takes the
last. Measured:

  * two non-null `systemInstruction` members are refused outright —
    `oneof field '_system_instruction' is already set`. Nothing is sent,
    so nothing is "discarded".
  * two non-null `toolConfig` members return 200 and *merge*: a request
    whose `tool_choice` allowed only `get_weather` and whose blob allowed
    only `get_time` called **both**. The narrower restriction does not
    lose to the wider one — it stops restricting anything, which is the
    worse outcome and the one worth naming.

Also pinned, after measuring it rather than assuming: a blob field is
emitted *beside* its typed `null`, and Gemini accepts that — a `null`
claims no oneof, so `{"toolConfig":null,"toolConfig":{…}}` returns 200
with the allow-list honoured. It reads like a bug and is not. Fixing it
means `skip_serializing_if` on two fields, which would drop
`"systemInstruction":null` from every recorded request body and
invalidate the cassette corpus, so the cell says that: if it fails, the
answer is a deliberate re-record, not a passing test.

And the pass-through cell's `videoMetadata` case is now a part kind rig
genuinely lacks. It previously used `inlineData`, which `PartKind` does
model — under the reverted implementation that case failed only because
`Content::role` re-serialized as an added `null`, i.e. for a reason a
plausible cleanup would have silently removed.

fix(openai-compatible): let llama.cpp receive an image in a tool result, plus two cassette-hygiene bugs (#2380)

* test(cassettes): scrub the local model path llama.cpp echoes on every response

A locally-hosted provider echoes the path it was launched with.
`llama-server` puts the whole thing in `model` on **every** chat
response:

    "model":"/Users/<name>/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--<org>--<repo>/snapshots/<sha>/<file>.gguf"

Recording one turn against it therefore writes the operator's username,
their cache layout and a snapshot hash into a fixture destined for a
public repository. Nothing in the scrubber reached it — it is not a
token, not a header, not a query parameter — and it trips no
`FORBIDDEN_CASSETTE_PATTERNS` entry, so the safety scan passed a fixture
carrying a home directory. Verified by recording one and grepping it.

The basename survives, because it is the useful and non-identifying half
(which model the fixture was recorded against) and a cell may reasonably
assert on it. Everything to its left is replaced.

The match is anchored to the start of a JSON string value, and that
anchor is the whole difference between a rule and a hazard. An
unanchored first version rewrote
`https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/physics/...` inside anthropic's recorded
web-search citations, corrupting three committed fixtures and failing
`cassettes_do_not_contain_obvious_secrets` with "not in scrubbed cassette
form". A real local path occupies the entire value; a URL that merely
contains `/home/` does not. Both cases are pinned, along with
idempotence — the safety check re-scrubs its own output, so a
non-idempotent rule fails there rather than here.

* test(cache): correct two cache exemptions that were false on both counts

`NO_CACHE_SUITE` excused llamafile and llamacpp from cache-prefix
coverage on the grounds that "the local llama.cpp wire reports no
cached-token field, so rig has no cache mapping for it". Both halves are
wrong, and each is falsifiable in a minute.

The wire reports it. Against `llama-server` b1-6d05498, sending the same
prefix twice with `cache_prompt` comes back with
`usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` at 28 of 29 prompt tokens,
and `timings.cache_n` agreeing.

And rig maps it: `openai::Usage::to_normalized` reads
`prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` into rig's usage, which llamafile
inherits along with the rest of the shared OpenAI-compatible layer.

The exemptions stay — no llama.cpp server runs in this environment, which
is the same reason `mistralrs` is exempt — but they now say that, so the
next person to read the list learns that a suite is worth building rather
than that there is nothing to assert. A stale justification is worse than
none: it answers the question that would otherwise get asked.

* feat(openai-compatible): let a provider that honours an image in a tool result send one

rig refused an image in a tool result unconditionally:

    message::ToolResultContent::Image(_) => Err(ConversionError(
      "OpenAI Chat Completions does not support images in tool results…"))

The refusal is right for OpenAI and wrong as a universal rule, and it
lives in a conversion nine providers share — so a llama.cpp user was told
about a limitation of a different vendor's API and denied a feature their
server has.

**llama.cpp honours it.** Measured against `llama-server` built from
source at commit `6d05498` running Qwen3-VL-2B: a solid-colour square
handed back through a `role:"tool"` message is named correctly for
magenta, green and yellow — 3/3 — matching a control that sends the
identical bytes in a `user` message in the same run. The image reaches
the model; only the message role differs between subject and control.

**Official OpenAI does not**, which is why the default stays `false`.
Chat Completions answers 400 on `gpt-4o`/`gpt-4o-mini` ("Image URLs are
only allowed for messages with role 'user'"), and on `gpt-5` … `gpt-5.5`
answers **200 with the image discarded**, the model then describing what
it never received. The second is worse than the first: a caller checking
status codes concludes the feature works.

So the capability is a per-provider constant beside its siblings —
`SUPPORTS_TOOLS`, `SUPPORTS_RESPONSE_FORMAT`,
`EMITS_COMPLETE_SINGLE_CHUNK_TOOL_CALLS` — and llamafile sets it. That is
what `providers/mod.rs` asks for: dialect differences belong in the
trait's hooks, never in the shared conversion.

The refusal moves to where the provider is known. `TryFrom<ToolResult>`
receives only the tool result, which is why the old guard had to be
unconditional; the per-provider normalization pass over `full_history`
already had the capabilities in hand. An unsupported image is refused
there rather than flattened, because `as_text()` would drop it and send a
tool result that silently says less than the caller asked for.

Three things the obvious refactor gets wrong, avoided here:

  * `to_array()` still lifts a `String` into an array, so
    `with_tool_result_array_content()` keeps working for the single-text
    case — which, since `TryFrom` flattens a lone text part to a string,
    is the common one.
  * `Deserialize` is hand-written rather than derived from the
    `tag = "type"`. The struct this enum replaced carried
    `#[serde(default)] r#type`, so a stored history whose parts omit
    `type` still loads; a derived tagged enum makes the tag mandatory and
    `ToolResultContentValue`'s `untagged` swallows the cause into "data
    did not match any variant".
  * `detail` and the media type survive the round trip.

An image also forces array content regardless of the flattening flag,
since a string has nowhere to put one.

* test(llamafile): record an image reaching the model through a tool result

Two cells, recorded in one run against `llama-server` built from source
at commit `6d05498` (`build_info` b1-6d05498) with
`ggml-org/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct-GGUF` Q8_0 and its mmproj, `--jinja --seed
42 --temp 0`.

The subject hands a magenta square back through a `role:"tool"` message
and asserts the model names the colour. The control sends the identical
bytes in a `user` message. Both are in one fixture directory on purpose:
the subject alone would prove only that something produced a colour word,
and the pair holds the image, the model and the run constant so the only
variable is the message role.

The assertion is the colour rather than a 200, because a cell that
checked acceptance would pass against a server that took the image and
dropped it — which is exactly what OpenAI's GPT-5 family does, and the
failure most worth catching.

Magenta on purpose: "red" and "blue" are plausible blind guesses for the
dominant colour of an image, and magenta is not. (The 2B model calls it
"pink", which the assertion accepts.)

* docs(changelog): record the image-tool-result capability flag

* fix: six defects a cold review found in this branch

Three of them mattered, and one would have been a red CI job.

**A broken intra-doc link.** `ToolResultContentValue::as_text`'s doc
pointed at `[`Self::normalize_for_wire`]`, a method that never existed —
that logic was inlined into `TryFrom<OpenAIRequestParams>` instead. CI
runs `cargo doc` with `RUSTDOCFLAGS: -D warnings`, so an unresolved link
is an error, and `cargo doc` was the one check missing from this branch's
verification list. Reproduced, then fixed by naming the location in prose
rather than linking a symbol.

**The scrub rule left the home-directory name behind.** Ending the path
at the first whitespace splits a home directory that contains one:
`/Users/John Smith/models/m.gguf` scrubbed to
`/REDACTED_PATH/John Smith/models/m.gguf`, keeping `John` as the
"basename" and copying the rest through verbatim. macOS creates exactly
that shape from a full account name. The output is a fixed point of the
rule, so re-scrubbing — which is how the safety scan checks — reports
nothing. A rule that looks like it closes a leak and does not is worse
than no rule. The path now ends at the closing quote of its JSON string
and nowhere else.

**The inbound conversion dropped images the outbound one preserves.**
`TryFrom<Message> for message::Message` flattened tool-result content
through `as_text()`, which now skips image parts — so a wire tool result
carrying an image came back as `Text("")`. That is the same silent loss
the outbound gate exists to refuse, and worse here because it used to be
impossible: before `ToolResultContent` grew an image variant such a body
failed to deserialize, so the loss was at least loud.
`into_message_content` carries every part back, images included.

Also: the refusal message was a wrapped string literal without `\`
continuations, so four runs of ~30 spaces reached the user; the error
arms Debug-printed `DocumentSourceKind`, which for `Raw(Vec<u8>)` dumps a
whole image into an error string; and the enum change is a breaking one
(`ToolResultContent.text` and `ToolResultContentType` are gone,
`OpenAIRequestParams` gained a field) that the changelog filed only under
`Added`.

Four new cells: the space-in-home-directory case, and the inbound round
trip for an image-only and a mixed tool result.

test(llamacpp, llamafile): bring all 53 ignored llama.cpp tests under recorded coverage (#2381)

Two suites described behaviour that nothing had ever run. 23 tests in
`tests/providers/llamacpp/` drove a raw `openai::Client` at
`localhost:8080` with no cassettes at all, and 30 more in the llamafile
suite were live-only, covering areas — structured output, extractors,
request hooks, permission control, loaders, context — that had no
recorded twin. All 53 carried `#[ignore]`. None remain.

Recorded against `llama-server` built from source at commit `0329fcd`
running `unsloth/Qwen3-1.7B-GGUF` Q4_K_M with `--jinja --seed 42
--temp 0 -c 4096` (plus `--embeddings --pooling mean` for the embeddings
cells; llama.cpp answers `Pooling type 'none' is not OAI compatible`
without it). 23 new llamacpp fixtures, 15 new llamafile ones.

The llamacpp suite drives llama.cpp through the **generic**
OpenAI-compatible client rather than through `providers::llamafile`, and
keeping both is deliberate: llamafile overrides `build_uri` to append
`/v1` and cannot send an `Authorization` header at all, so a defect in
one path is invisible to the other.

Four bugs the conversion exposed, each of which had been sitting behind
an `#[ignore]`:

**Tool-calling cells never had enough turns.** Five cells call a tool
under `stream_prompt`/`prompt_typed`, whose default is a single turn — so
the tool result had nowhere to go and the run died with
`MaxTurnsError { max_turns: 1 }`. The llamafile cassette twin of one of
them has always passed `max_turns(4)`; these copies had simply never run.

**Two cells fought over one file.** Both `permission_control` cells wrote
and then deleted `test.txt` in the process's working directory. Run
concurrently — the default — one cell's `Drop` deleted the file the other
was midway through reading, `head`/`tail` returned nothing, the tool
result changed and the recorded body stopped matching. It reproduced 4
runs out of 4 in the full suite and passed 4 of 4 in isolation, which is
shared state rather than flakiness. Each cell now owns a `ScratchFile` in
the temp dir; the tool *descriptions* still say "test.txt", so the
recorded request bodies are unchanged.

**The batch extractor needs unordered matching.** `multi_extract` issues
its requests concurrently, so the order they reach the mock varies; under
ordered matching an early request consumed an interaction meant for a
later one and the last request found nothing whose body matched.

**Four llamafile cells were exact duplicates** of an existing cassette
cell of the same name (`agent::completion_smoke`,
`embeddings::embeddings_smoke`, `streaming::streaming_smoke`,
`streaming_tools::streaming_tools_smoke`). They are deleted rather than
converted: the cassette version already ran, so the live copy was dead
weight that could only drift.

Also: `skip_if_server_unavailable()` is gone from every converted cell —
a replayed cassette always has a server, so the guard was dead code that
would have silently skipped the suite. And `CASSETTE_CHAT_MODEL`'s doc
now says what it is: llama.cpp ignores `model` and serves whatever GGUF
it was launched with, so the constant is a label the harness matches on,
not a selector — which is why fixtures recorded against Ollama and
against llama.cpp can share it.

Co-authored-by: Lars Weber <lars@inqode.solutions>

feat(llamacpp)!: replace the llamafile provider, merge its two suites, and exhaust the matrix (#2382)

* feat(llamacpp): replace the llamafile provider, merging its two test suites into one

`providers::llamafile` is deleted and `providers::llamacpp` takes its place:
same server, the name people search for. A `.llamafile` serves the same
OpenAI-compatible API from the same llama.cpp core, so one provider covers
both.

Three limitations of the provider being replaced are closed:

* an optional API key, so a `llama-server --api-key` deployment is reachable
  at all. The old `ApiKey` type was `Nothing`, which cannot produce an
  `Authorization` header by construction;
* four capability slots instead of two — completion, embeddings, model
  listing and rerank — with a stated reason on each of the three left as
  `Nothing`. Rerank needed a shared Jina-shaped driver, which did not exist;
* `build_uri` no longer appends `/v1` unconditionally, so the base URL from
  the module's own doc line stops producing `/v1/v1`.

The two test suites recording the same scenarios through different clients
are merged into one: 61 fixtures become 42, with 19 name-colliding duplicates
dropped in favour of the provider path. The bare-`openai::Client`-against-a-
local-server path survives as a deliberately small suite covering only what
differs between the two.

* test(llamacpp): re-record the merged corpus against one pinned server

Every fixture in the merged suite now comes from the same `llama-server`
build (b10499, commit 6d05498) with generation pinned (`--seed 42 --temp 0`),
and each cell's module doc names the model, quant and server invocation it was
recorded under. The pre-merge corpus mixed three request-model strings and two
build tags, and the embeddings cells had been recorded against Ollama's
`all-minilm` while claiming to be llama.cpp coverage; they now run against a
real embedding model (`Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B-GGUF` Q8_0) on an
`--embeddings --pooling mean` server.

Two test defects surfaced by actually recording these cells rather than
replaying them:

* `raw_capture_matrix::normalized_fields_equal_raw_renormalized` compared a
  live `model` against the recorded one. llama.cpp echoes the loaded GGUF's
  filesystem path there and the scrubber rewrites it on the way to disk, so
  the cell could never pass on a recording pass — it had only ever replayed.
* the bare-`openai::Client` cells used a `const` for their scenario strings,
  which the cassette-safety scan reads off the AST and therefore could not see.

* test(llamacpp): the error matrix, and the verify path it corrected

Nothing in rig had recorded a single non-2xx response from llama.cpp: both
pre-merge corpora were happy paths end to end. Fourteen cells now cross ten
failure classes with the server configuration each needs, asserting the
status class and the preserved envelope rather than any literal id, and
reading the recorded bytes back to prove each premise.

Two behaviours are worth naming. llama.cpp reports `tools` without `--jinja`
as `500 server_error` although the caller caused it, so a client that retries
5xx will retry forever. And an unknown model is not an error at all: the
field is decorative on a single-model server, so a typo answers from whatever
is loaded.

Recording the verify cell found that `/v1/props` is a 404 — llama.cpp serves
its operational routes off the server root, not the `/v1` namespace — so
`build_uri` now keeps that namespace unprefixed from either accepted spelling
of the base URL. `VERIFY_PATH` is `/props` rather than the `/models` the old
provider used because `/v1/models` and `/health` are the only two routes
llama.cpp serves *without* the API-key check: verifying against `/models`
returns 200 for a wrong key.

* feat(llamacpp): preserve `timings`, which the shared OpenAI response type drops

llama.cpp reports server-side latency accounting beside `usage` on every chat
completion — `prompt_ms`, `predicted_ms`, `predicted_per_second`, `cache_n`.
It is the only such accounting a caller gets, and for local inference
tokens-per-second is the number people actually watch.

`openai::CompletionResponse` has neither a field for it nor a catch-all, so a
provider whose `Response` is that type drops it. The *streaming* path does not:
`StreamingCompletionChunk` carries a `#[serde(flatten)]` catch-all precisely so
"raw_stream must not erase them merely because the shared wire shape does not
know their names yet". `llamacpp::CompletionResponse` removes that asymmetry
for this provider, following the precedent deepseek and mira set, by flattening
the OpenAI payload and adding a typed `Timings` beside it; every trait a
`Response` must satisfy delegates to the OpenAI half so the wrapper cannot
drift from the shared conversion.

Both halves of the asymmetry are now pinned against recorded bytes:
`raw_capture_matrix::raw_preserves_the_timings_the_openai_type_drops` asserts
the field survives *and* that reading the same fixture as
`openai::CompletionResponse` loses it, and
`raw_stream_capture_matrix::stream_raw_preserves_llamacpp_timings` asserts the
streaming path carries it under `additional_params`.

The fields llama.cpp does not put on this wire are stated rather than assumed:
`tokens_evaluated`, `tokens_cached`, `truncated`, `stop_type`, `stopping_word`
and `generation_settings` exist only on the native `POST /completion`, which
rig never calls.

* test(llamacpp): the tool matrix, and the tool_choice llama.cpp silently ignores

Twelve cells cross arity (0/1/3 tools, parallel), a failing tool, all four
tool_choice modes, and tool results carrying text and JSON. The core cells run
on the competent tier (`unsloth/Qwen3-8B-GGUF` Q4_K_M) because a 1.7B declines
tool calls often enough that "the model refused" and "rig dropped the tools"
are indistinguishable from the outside.

Two behaviours the matrix found:

`tool_choice` naming a specific function is not representable on this wire.
`llama-server` reads the field with
`json_value(body, "tool_choice", std::string("auto"))` — as a *string* — and
its vocabulary is exactly auto/none/required
(`common_chat_tool_choice_parse_oaicompat`, common/chat.cpp:344). An
OpenAI-shaped object type-mismatches that read and falls through to the
default, so the request runs as `auto`: measured on b10499-6d05498 with both
tiers, naming `subtract` while the prompt asks for an addition calls `add`.
`LlamacppExt::prepare_request` now refuses it locally, naming the tool and
pointing at `ToolChoice::Required`, which llama.cpp does honour — the same
rule `SUPPORTS_IMAGE_TOOL_RESULTS` follows for the same reason.

`tool_choice: "none"` leaves the tool definitions in the rendered prompt and
only switches off the parser, so a model that calls one anyway emits its
template's raw `<tool_call>…</tool_call>` syntax as assistant text. That is
llama.cpp's behaviour and rig passing it through verbatim is right; the cell
records the shape so it is not mistaken for a rig defect later.

* test(llamacpp): the structured-output matrix, and llama.cpp's schema/grammar hole

Six cells across the four ways to constrain an answer. Two are findings about
llama.cpp rather than about rig, and both are silent:

`response_format: {"type": "json_object"}` constrains **nothing**. llama.cpp
derives `json_schema` from `response_format["schema"]`, so a bare
`json_object` with no schema key yields the empty schema `{}` — which matches
every JSON value and, compiled to GBNF, admits anything. The answer comes back
as markdown-fenced prose no JSON parser accepts. Rig never sends a bare
`json_object` (`output_schema` maps to `json_schema`, which *is* enforced),
so this is a trap for `additional_params` callers rather than a rig defect.

The schema/grammar conflict guard has a hole on exactly the route rig uses.
`if (!json_schema.is_null() && !grammar.empty()) throw` reads the *top-level*
`json_schema` field and runs before `response_format` is unpacked into the
same variable, so a top-level schema plus a grammar is a 500 while
`response_format` plus a grammar passes and the schema silently wins. Both
sides are recorded.

Also pinned: a GBNF grammar reaches the wire verbatim through
`additional_params`, and a schema-constrained turn on the smoke tier cannot
escape its grammar even when the prompt explicitly tells the model to.

* test(llamacpp): the content and cross-family matrices, and the streaming const they disproved

`EMITS_COMPLETE_SINGLE_CHUNK_TOOL_CALLS` is now `false`. The const asks
whether the backend can put a whole tool call — id, name and *complete*
arguments — into one streaming chunk, and this provider inherited `true`.
Measured against llama-server b10499-6d05498 it is false on every template
that can call a tool at all: arguments stream one token at a time, so the
first chunk carries the name beside a lone `{` and the closing `}` arrives
ten chunks later. Even a zero-argument call streams as `{` then `}`.

Re-measured across four families — Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.2-3B and
Mistral-Small-3.2-24B — with one blocking and one streaming cell per non-Qwen
family, which is where a template difference would show. Gemma 3 declares
`chat_template_caps.supports_tool_calls: false` and answers a tool prompt with
a ```tool_code block as prose; that is a capability the model lacks, recorded
as a note with its streaming twin dropped for the stated reason.

Flipping the const changes no output and that is checked, not argued: the
shared accumulator's immediate-emit is a probe (`UnparseableToolInput::Keep`)
that finalizes a call only when its accumulated arguments parse, so a lone
`{` was already declined — all 150 recorded cells replay byte-identically
either way.

The content matrix adds five cells: an answer wholly consumed by a stop
sequence (a 200 on the wire that rig turns into the shared
`EMPTY_RESPONSE_ERROR` — deliberate, and now debuggable), consecutive
same-role messages arriving unmerged, multi-byte characters surviving SSE
chunking, an 8 KiB tool result reaching the model intact, and a system message
keeping its place at the head of a history.

* test(llamacpp): the prompt-caching suite that removes the NO_CACHE_SUITE exemption

`tests/cassette_cache_prefix.rs` carried an exemption for both llama.cpp
suites reading "records against a local llama.cpp server that is not running
in this environment". A server is running for this PR, so the exemption is
deleted and five recorded cells replace it.

llama.cpp's cache is the server's own KV slot cache rather than a hosted
prefix cache: it caches from the first token, needs no opt-in, and reports its
work in two independently populated places —
`usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, which rig normalizes, and
`timings.cache_n`, which this provider now preserves. Measured on
b10499-6d05498: a 2,825-token prefix re-sent reads 2,824 back, and a fifth
cell asserts the two counters agree turn by turn across three scenarios.

`cache_prompt: false` is a llama.cpp-only request field and rides
`additional_params`. Its cell pins both halves: the turn reads zero cached
tokens, and it does **not** evict the slot — the turn after it hits again, so
"disable caching for this one prompt" does not cost the conversation.

Two properties of a server-side cache the harness had not met before, both
handled rather than papered over: each cell gets its own probe label, because
cells sharing a preamble share a KV slot and the second one's turn 1 would
already be warm; and the probe uses 100 padding repetitions rather than the
default 180, because the recording server's `-c 4096` cannot hold a
4,700-token probe (Groq's suite reduces padding for the same kind of reason).

* test(llamacpp): the rerank matrix and the unmapped-surface decisions

Reranking is the capability slot this PR adds, and it now has its own matrix
against a real cross-encoder (`gpustack/bge-reranker-v2-m3-GGUF` Q4_K_M on an
`--embeddings --pooling rank --reranking` server): multi-document ordering,
a single document, `top_n` above and below the document count. The empty list
and the no-reranker-loaded cases live in the error matrix.

`RerankResult::relevance_score` documented itself as "between 0 and 1".
llama.cpp returns the cross-encoder's raw logit — 0.2516, -4.761 and -8.377
for three documents against "What is a panda?" — so the doc was wrong the
moment a second implementation existed. Corrected to state the only real
guarantee (higher is more relevant, comparable within one response), with the
measurement cited and a cell that keeps the new wording honest.

Part 3's remaining routes are decided rather than left open. Recorded:
`GET /v1/models` really does return a hybrid body — an Ollama-style `models`
array beside OpenAI's `object:"list"`/`data`, keyed on `name` and `id`
respectively — and rig reads the OpenAI half; `GET /props` carries the build
tag and modalities a fixture is identified by; `POST /v1/responses` works end
to end through a bare `openai::Client`, so excluding it is "one provider, one
wire" rather than "rig cannot"; and `POST /v1/audio/transcriptions` answers
501 on any model without an audio projector, which is what makes declaring the
transcription slot the wrong call. `/infill`, `/v1/messages`, the legacy
completion wire and the operational routes are excluded with their reasons in
the module docs.

* test(llamacpp): the multimodal matrix, on two vision tiers chosen by measurement

Six cells: two images in one turn keeping their order, an image beside a tool,
a malformed data URI, an unfetchable image URL, an image to a server with no
`--mmproj`, and a video part.

The two vision models fail in opposite directions and each cell says which it
needs. Asked which of two images is the photograph, Qwen3-VL-2B answers FIRST
whichever order they arrive in — responsive but not tracking order — while
Qwen2.5-VL-7B answers FIRST and SECOND correctly, so multi-image ordering runs
on the larger one and records *both* orders in one scenario (a single order
would pass on a model that ignored the images). Asked to call a tool about an
image, the smaller model calls it and the larger writes prose, because
Qwen2.5-VL's template reports `supports_tool_calls: false` with or without an
image — so image-plus-tools stays on the smaller model.

`GET /props` advertises `modalities.video: true` on both, which made "what
does rig do with a video part" a real question. Rig maps
`UserContent::Video` to OpenAI's `video_url` part and llama.cpp answers
`400 unsupported content[].type`: the flag describes what the model can
encode, not what the chat-completions content vocabulary accepts. A recorded
boundary, not a defect.

Two more caller errors llama.cpp reports as 5xx: an unfetchable image URL and
a missing `--mmproj`, joining `--no-jinja` with tools and the schema/grammar
conflict.

* docs(llamacpp): the breaking change, the migration, and the suite's matrix index

CHANGELOG gains the rename as a breaking Added entry plus four Fixed entries;
MIGRATING gains a 0.41 → next section covering the module rename, the four
behaviours that are not renames (an API key is now possible, `from_env` no
longer demands a base URL, a `/v1` base URL is no longer doubled, and a
specific-function `tool_choice` is refused rather than silently downgraded),
the `raw_completion` return type change, and the corrected
`relevance_score` documentation. Historical CHANGELOG entries are untouched:
past releases did ship a provider called `llamafile`.

The suite's `mod.rs` now carries the index the per-file tables hang off: the
fourteen server configurations with their exact invocations, which dimension
lives in which module, the model-tier escalation rule, and the five dimensions
deliberately not recorded with a reason each.

* fix(llamacpp): broken intra-doc links, a needless borrow, and a fixture the safety scan could not see

Three verification failures, each caught by the check that gets skipped:

* `cargo doc` with `-D rustdoc::broken-intra-doc-links` rejected three links
  in the new provider — a trait method addressed as an inherent one, a private
  const, and a trait associated const. CI runs `RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings cargo
  doc --locked --no-deps --all-features`, which is stricter still and now
  passes.
* clippy's `needless_borrows_for_generic_args` on the bare-openai wrapper.
* the transcription cell called `ProviderCassette::start` directly, so the
  cassette-safety scan — which reads wrapper names off the AST — reported its
  fixture orphaned. It now goes through a registered
  `with_llamacpp_raw_http_cassette`, which is the honest shape anyway: the
  cell reaches a route no rig capability addresses, and that is the point.

* test(llamacpp): make the table-vs-tests audit a guard instead of a one-off

The triple-verification step asks for each matrix table to be checked
row-for-row against the test binary's `--list` output. Doing that by hand
once catches today's drift and nothing after it, so it is a test now:
`matrix_index` reads the same source the tables live in and asserts that every
matrix module names all of its own cells, that the suite index in `mod.rs`
mentions every module under `cassette/`, and that `mod.rs`'s declaration list
matches the directory so a file cannot exist without being compiled.

It found three gaps on its first run: two matrix cells with no table row
(`verify_fails_without_the_key_and_succeeds_with_it`,
`the_smoke_tier_round_trip_is_covered_elsewhere`) and six migrated smoke
modules the suite index never mentioned. All three are fixed, and the
migrated-smoke modules now have their own index table.

Modules that are not matrices opt out by name in `NOT_TABULATED`, with a
staleness check on that list, so adding a new untabulated module is an
explicit decision rather than an omission.

* fix(embeddings): a declared width the provider ignores is now caught, not reported

Sweep 1 finding. `llama-server`'s embeddings handler reads no `dimensions`
field at all — the string does not appear anywhere under `tools/server/` — so
a request asking for 128 answers 200 with the loaded model's 1,024-wide
vectors. Rig went on reporting `ndims() == 128`.

That number is what a vector store sizes its index from, so the mismatch
surfaces far from the call that caused it, as an index that cannot hold its
own vectors, with nothing in the response saying anything was wrong. Confirmed
on origin/main: `ndims()` reports 128, vectors are 1024 wide, no error.

Fixed at both layers involved.

The shared OpenAI-compatible embeddings driver now compares an **explicitly
declared** width against the width that came back and raises
`EmbeddingError::MismatchedDimensions`. Only explicit declarations are
checked: a handle built without one reports whatever the provider's table says
and has nothing to disagree with. This is the shared layer because the root
cause is — the driver trusted a request field not every server honours, and
the servers where it matters are the ones that *ignore* it rather than
rejecting it. Blast radius is five in-crate unit tests whose stub bodies
declared one width and returned three floats; no cassette needed re-recording.
OpenAI's own `ada-002` is one of the affected models and its cell now records
both halves: `dimensions` never reaches the wire, and a width ada cannot
produce is refused.

`LlamacppExt::embedding_dimensions` stops sending the field, because putting a
claim on the wire that the wire ignores misleads whoever reads it next. The
caller's declaration is still meaningful — it is a statement about the loaded
GGUF — and a wrong one now fails loudly.

* test(llamacpp): the response-shape matrix — reasoning, n>1, logprobs, finish reasons

Four dimensions the generation matrices did not own.

`reasoning_content` is a field OpenAI does not define and llama.cpp populates
on both transports. The cell is a *parity* check rather than a shape check:
the two deliver it at different granularities — one `Reasoning` block when
blocking, a run of correlated `ReasoningDelta`s when streaming, which is rig's
normal streaming shape — and what matters is that neither lets it fall into
the plain-text surface, which is the failure the blocking mapping's own
comment says it exists to prevent. It does not, on either.

`n > 1` is one of the few places the shared candidate-selection rule is
observable: most providers reject it or are never asked, while llama.cpp
returns real interleaved candidates on both transports. The cell asserts the
blocking answer and the streamed index-0 candidate are the same text, having
first checked the recorded frames really do interleave two indices.

`logprobs` survive into `raw` and stay out of the normalized view.

The finish-reason dimension is *closed*, and the cell says so with evidence:
`server-task.cpp` builds the field from exactly `length`, `stop` and
`tool_calls`, so the cell sweeps the whole recorded corpus and requires each
to appear — failing both if one is missing and if a fourth ever shows up.

* test(llamacpp): the output-budget truncation matrix, a third wire for the #2359 policy

#2359 established a shared decoder policy for a turn that ran out of output
budget mid-arguments: tolerate unparseable tool-call arguments only when the
outer finish reason maps to `Length`, drop the unusable call, keep the rest of
the turn. It was derived from DeepSeek and Mistral.

llama.cpp produces exactly that state from a completely different server and
nothing had checked the policy against it. Measured on b10499-6d05498 with
`tool_choice: required`, the cut lands where the budget runs out: 12 tokens
gives `{`, 20 gives `{"note": "The`, 28 gives 60 characters of it. Three
cells — blocking, streaming, and a control with room to finish, without which
the first two would pass against a provider that had simply stopped calling
the tool. The policy holds on all three.

* test(llamacpp): two more cells sweep 1 turned up

An embeddings input larger than the server's *physical batch* is a 500 naming
that limit — a different limit from the context window, with a different
remedy (`-b`/`--ubatch-size`, not `-c`), and the fourth caller error in this
corpus that arrives as a 5xx. Recorded so a reader who sees "too large to
process" does not reach for the wrong flag.

And the `response_format`-with-tools deferral, measured against a server where
the consequence of not deferring is total. A schema compiles to a grammar
applied during sampling, and that grammar admits only schema-shaped JSON — so
a request carrying both answers `{"city": "Paris"}` with no tool call at all,
however clearly the prompt asks for a lookup. The shared builder already
withholds `response_format` until a tool result exists; the cell asserts the
tool reached the wire, the schema did not, and the call still happened.

* test(llamacpp): the turn-termination matrix, a cross-provider dimension llama.cpp lacked

Sweep 2 found the gap rather than a bug: `ModelTurnFinished` carries the
normalized finish reason and the effective output cap for each attempt
(rig#2184 / #2341), Anthropic, Gemini and OpenAI each have a recorded matrix
for it, and llama.cpp had none — despite being a provider whose whole
vocabulary is reachable without asking a model to misbehave.

Five cells: `Length` with its cap on both surfaces, `Stop` failing the retry
predicate, `ToolCalls` on a tool turn, and the escalation loop — a tiny cap
truncates, a provider-neutral hook reads `Length` and repeats with a larger
one, and each attempt reports its own post-patch cap rather than the agent's
baseline. Both attempts live in one cassette, and the recorded caps and
reasons are asserted in order so the hook's account and the wire's agree.

The vocabulary is closed here — `server-task.cpp` builds the field from
exactly `stop`, `length` and `tool_calls` — so there is no `ContentFilter`,
no `Other(_)` and no absent reason to reach, and the corpus-wide sweep in
`response_shape_matrix` fails if a fourth value ever appears.

* test(llamacpp): response identity and typed-route parity, the last two universal dimensions

Sweep 2's second gap. `response_identity_edge` and
`raw_completion_parity_matrix` exist in six and five other provider suites
respectively; llama.cpp had neither.

`provider_request_id` is `None` here, and the cell makes that a measurement
rather than a default nobody checked: llama-server b10499 stamps no id header
on any route, on either transport. The assertion runs against the *recorded*
headers, which matters because the cassette policy's allowlist explicitly
keeps `request-id`, `x-request-id` and `mistral-correlation-id` — so an empty
result is the server's silence, not the scrubber's, and the day llama.cpp
starts sending one the cell says so and names `REQUEST_ID_HEADER`.

The body-level `chatcmpl-…` id is a different thing with a different lifetime,
and does reach the caller on both transports.

Parity follows from the first fact: because there is no transport id for
`raw_completion` to drop, the plain typed route already reproduces the
normalized one field for field — which is why this provider needs none of the
`raw_completion_with_request_id` machinery Groq and xAI do. Recorded rather
than assumed.

* test(llamacpp): the additional_params precedence rule half this matrix depends on

Sweep 3. `stop`, `seed`, `grammar`, `n` and `logprobs` have no typed home in
rig's `CompletionRequest`, so every cell that exercises them reaches the wire
through `additional_params` — which makes "what happens when the blob names a
field the builder also set" load-bearing for reading any of those fixtures.
Nothing stated it.

The escape hatch wins: the typed fields serialize first and the flattened map
is written over them, so `max_tokens(7)` plus an `additional_params` carrying
`max_tokens: 99` sends 99, with no warning. Defensible for an escape hatch,
and worth writing down. Definitional rather than observed, so the cell needs
no server.

Also notes the streaming 401 as a deliberate drop: llama.cpp's API-key
middleware runs before the handler, so a `stream: true` request without the
key answers the same body before any event stream opens. The streaming error
path is covered where it actually differs — the context-overflow cell, whose
400 has to survive rig's SSE funnel.

* test(llamacpp): the tool_choice refusal applies on the streaming path too

A guard covering one surface would be worse than none — a caller moving from
`completion` to `stream` would silently get the old behaviour back.
`prepare_request` is invoked by both paths; this makes that a checked fact
rather than a reading of the source.

* fix: the ten findings a cold review of this branch turned up

A fresh subagent reviewed the diff with no context. It found no bug in the new
provider code and ten real defects elsewhere; all ten are fixed.

**The embeddings width check was too broad and undocumented.** It fired on
`ndims == 0` — rig's sentinel for *unknown*, produced by `default_ndims`
returning `None` and by `GenericEmbeddingModel::new(client, model, 0)` — which
would have turned every such handle into a hard error on its first request.
Zero is now carved out, with a unit test. And the change is breaking for every
OpenAI-compatible embeddings provider, which neither CHANGELOG nor MIGRATING
said: both now carry it, along with the `VERIFY_PATH` move from `/v1/models`
to `/props`, which breaks a proxy that only forwards `/v1/*`.

**Three cells could not fail for the reason they named.** The `n > 1` cell
compared two fixtures to each other and never looked at rig's output, while
its two candidates were byte-identical — a decoder selecting candidate 1 or
concatenating both passed green. It now samples at a temperature that makes
the candidates differ, asserts they differ, and compares rig's own answer to
candidate 0 on both transports. The finish-reason sweep only ever collected
strings from its own expected list, so `seen ⊆ expected` held by construction
and the "a fourth value would fail this" half was unenforceable; it now reads
whatever value is present. Both fixes were verified by mutation — injecting
`content_filter` into a fixture now fails the sweep.

**Two docs described a difference this PR itself removed.** `streaming_tools`
opened by saying it exercised "complete-single-chunk tool call streaming", the
exact claim measured false here, and `bare_openai_client`'s stream cell was
framed around a const that now has the same value on both paths. The first is
rewritten; the second is re-aimed at the reassembly claim, which is real and
which nothing else in that file covered.

**Weak assertions**: a derived `Debug` compared against the empty string, a
status check structurally true for the variant it followed, `unwrap_or_default`
letting a *missing* field pass an "incomplete" check, "arguments must be
complete" satisfied by the truncated sibling's value, and a loop introduced as
proving two images arrived "in order" that never compared the two orderings.
Each now asserts what its name says.

**Stale and mis-cited**: `Llamafile` still listed in `rig-core/src/lib.rs` and
`rig-core/README.md`; rerank scores quoted as `0.2516, -4.761, -8.377` in
three places including a public API doc when every fixture records `0.8225,
-4.7583, -8.3761`; a cache hit ratio quoted from a hand probe rather than the
fixtures the module records; a "third 5xx" that was the fifth; and a
zero-argument streaming claim asserted nowhere — now its own cell, reading the
fixture that already existed.

**One claim the suite's own standard required recording**: that `GET /v1/models`
answers 200 without a credential on a keyed server. It is the whole
justification for moving `VERIFY_PATH`, and it is now a cell, asserted beside
the 401 the same client gets from the same server for anything else.

* test(llamacpp): sweep 4 — the top_n zero arm and the rerank decode-error path

No new bug. Two gaps closed.

`top_n: 0` completes the third arm of that dimension, and is the one where a
clamp implemented as `min(top_n, len)` could plausibly have gone the other way
and treated zero as "unset". It does not — and 0 has to reach the wire rather
than being dropped as falsy, which the cell asserts.

And the one path in the new shared rerank driver a live server cannot produce:
a 200 whose body is not a ranking. llama.cpp always answers the Jina shape, so
the case only arises behind a proxy — and without the provider label the caller
gets a bare serde message with no indication of which server produced it, on a
driver that is shared by construction.

* test(llamacpp): sweep 5 — a mechanical scan for assertions that cannot fail

No new bug, and the last two unfalsifiable assertions are gone.

The sweep was a script rather than a reading: scan every cell for
`!format!("{x:?}").is_empty()`, `assert!(true)`, `assert_eq!(x, x)` and
or-true patterns, and separately check every one of the 143 fixtures carries a
`when`/`then` pair, a status and a non-empty response body. The fixtures were
clean; the scan found one `Debug`-never-empty assertion whose earlier fix had
silently not applied, and one cell whose only post-replay assertion restated
its own input.

The reasoning cell now extracts the block's text and requires it non-empty —
verified by mutation: forcing the extraction to yield `""` fails it. The
auth cell's coda now asserts something about the *recorder* instead of about
its own input: that no fixture in this repository may contain an
`authorization` header, since it is not on `RECORDED_REQUEST_HEADERS` — which
is the stated reason that cell proves the header in process rather than from
the fixture. That needed a shared `recorded_request_header_pairs` reader,
beside the response-header one.

* feat(embeddings)!: normalize embedding responses; inherent raw_embed_texts on every provider

The last modality #2385 left unnormalized. `EmbeddingResponse` is now the
full normalized response — `embeddings`, `usage`, `provider`, `model`,
`response_id`, `provider_request_id`, `raw`, `identity()` — and
`EmbeddingModel::embed_texts_response` (renamed from `embed_texts_with_usage`,

provider implements; `embed_texts`, `embed_text` and `embed_text_response`
derive from it. The other direction is impossible: a default forwarding to

feat(telemetry): gen_ai spans for every non-completion modality, plus a recorded embedding matrix for all seven keyed providers (#2390)

* feat(telemetry): gen_ai spans for every non-completion modality

Completions were the only instrumented model calls; the normalized usage and
identity every modality response carries since the type-erasure sweep never
reached a span. Add `ModalityOperation` + `ModalitySpanBuilder` (operation
names embeddings / rerank / transcription / image_generation /
audio_generation on target `rig::modalities`) and one shared seam,
`telemetry::instrument_modality`, which opens the canonical span, runs the
call inside it, and records `gen_ai.usage.*`, `gen_ai.response.id` and
`gen_ai.response.model` off the normalized response on success.

Unlike `CompletionSpanBuilder`, modality spans never adopt an ambient span:
the adoption contract exists so one model *turn* has exactly one completion
span, and a modality call is not a turn — an agent's RAG lookup nests as its
own child span instead of overwriting the turn's fields.

Every provider implementation of `embed_texts_response`,
`embed_images_response`, `rerank`, `transcription`, `image_generation`
and `audio_generation` now routes through the seam — the shared OpenAI
embeddings/rerank/transcription/image/audio drivers cover their whole
compatible families at once, plus the hand-written seams (Cohere, Gemini
REST, Voyage, Ollama, Copilot, Hugging Face, Mistral, OpenRouter,
Hyperbolic) and the external crates (Bedrock, Gemini gRPC, FastEmbed).

The vector-store search path needs no store-side change: `embed_text` /
`embed_texts` are defaults derived from `embed_texts_response`, so a
`top_n` query records the same telemetry through the seam the model call
opens — pinned by a test driving `InMemoryVectorIndex::top_n` over the
OpenAI driver and counting the recorded usage fields.

driver read no header and every normalized embedding response reported
`provider_request_id: None` — the id Mistral support asks for, silently

Found while recording the embedding matrix; pinned by the recorded

refactor!: make websockets transport-agnostic — protocol to rig-core, socket to rig-tungstenite (#2426)

* refactor!: make websockets transport-agnostic — protocol to rig-core, socket to rig-tungstenite

The OpenAI Responses websocket mode lived in rig-reqwest because
tokio-tungstenite did. That put OpenAI *protocol* — the event envelopes, the
turn state machine, the previous_response_id chaining — inside the reqwest
transport crate, forced a TLS feature axis onto it that had nothing to do with
reqwest, and left the next provider's websocket support nowhere to go but
another transport-coupled module.

Split it the way HTTP already is: rig-core states the contract and owns the
protocol, a backend-named crate owns the socket.

- `rig_core::ws_client`: `WebSocketClientExt` (the backend), the object-safe
  `WebSocketConnection` (one socket, held erased so sessions keep a single
  generic parameter), `Frame`, and the shared http->ws URL derivation. Built
  from http/bytes/futures/url only — rig-core still pulls in no tokio, no
  reqwest and no tungstenite, with every feature on.
- `rig_core::providers::openai::responses_api::websocket`: the session,
  rewritten against `WebSocketConnection`. The two `tokio::time::timeout` calls
  become `wasm_compat::timeout`, which is why the module now builds for
  wasm32-unknown-unknown even though no wasm backend ships yet.
- `rig-tungstenite`: the binding — `connect_async`, the Frame <-> Message
  mapping, the rustls/native-tls axis, and the off-tokio-runtime path (the
  socket moves onto the fallback runtime as a request/response actor, so a
  caller on a Bevy task pool or smol polls only futures channels).

Upgrade-rejection fidelity is unchanged and now covered on both sides of the
seam plus end-to-end: the backend reports a refused upgrade as
`Error::non_success_with_details`, and the provider reads its own request-id
header back off it — so status, body, request id and rate-limit headers still
reach the caller (rig#2314, rig#2315, rig#2210). Reading OpenAI's header is
provider knowledge, and it now sits with the provider instead of the transport.

The ~2100 lines of session tests that needed a live server, TLS and a tokio
reactor to assert on protocol behaviour now run against an in-memory scripted
connection in rig-core; rig-tungstenite keeps the end-to-end suites (wire
conformance, handshake rejection, off-runtime).

`http_client::Error::non_success_status()` / `non_success_body()` become public:
a backend outside rig-core builds that error, and the provider layer reads it.

Through the `rig` facade the common path is unchanged — `websocket` +
`use rig::prelude::*` still gives `client.responses_websocket(..)`, now via
rig-tungstenite's DefaultWebSocketClient. MIGRATING.md carries the breaks.

* fix: make the off-runtime connection actor interruptible, and three review fixes

Review findings on #2426.

1. The off-runtime actor deadlocked. It was strictly serial, so a read command
   parked it in `stream.next()` until a frame arrived. When the session's event
   timeout fired, the caller dropped its `recv()` future but the actor stayed
   parked, and the `close()` that follows a timeout waited forever for a frame
   that was never coming. The same shape lost a frame whenever a caller
   cancelled a read (their own `select!`), which then hung the next read, and
   leaked the task and socket when the connection was dropped mid-read.

   The actor now reads and serves commands concurrently over a split socket:
   inbound frames are buffered as they arrive, a read is answered from that
   buffer, and a frame whose caller has gone away goes back on the front of it.
   A dropped command channel ends the task. Reading continuously also keeps
   tungstenite's automatic pong replies flowing.

   Both failure modes are now regression tests in `off_runtime.rs`, bounded so
   a regression fails rather than hangs, and both fail against the old actor.
   This is the assertion the in-memory port dropped: the pre-split suite had
   `event_timeout_rejects_reuse_and_allows_close` against a live server, and a
   scripted connection's `close()` always resolves, so rig-core's replacement
   cannot hold it — it belongs with the real backend.

2. `websocket-rustls` / `websocket-native-tls` were unusable alone: they
   enabled the backend crate but not the `websocket` gate the facade's
   re-exports sit behind, and `websocket` hard-wired rustls. `websocket` is now
   the API gate and takes its TLS stack from the workspace-wide `rustls` /
   `native-tls` features, as the HTTP transport does; the two `-tls` spellings
   select both at once. All three now work standalone, and
   `--no-default-features --features websocket-native-tls` gives a socket with
   no rustls in its tree.

3. The alias-completeness guard exempted any file named `websocket.rs`
   anywhere under the provider tree, so a future provider's ungated
   `websocket.rs` would have dropped out of it silently. It is exempted by
   exact path now.

4. `Message::Frame` was mapped to `Frame::Binary`, which would have fed a raw
   control frame to the JSON parser and failed the session on decode. It is
   skipped again, as before the split: `from_message` returns `Option<Frame>`.

* fix: restore TLS on the websocket feature, keep the session Sync, and three review fixes

Second review pass on #2426.

1. The previous commit's feature rework left `--no-default-features --features
   websocket` with no TLS stack at all: the facade declared rig-tungstenite
   `default-features = false`, so nothing enabled a tungstenite TLS backend and
   every `wss://` handshake failed at runtime with `Url(TlsFeatureNotEnabled)`.
   That combination worked on main. The dependency now keeps the backend's own
   `default = ["rustls"]`, so enabling `websocket` always yields a socket that
   can speak `wss://`.

   Additive features cannot express "replace rustls with native-tls", so
   `websocket-native-tls` through the facade compiles rustls as well; a
   native-tls-only socket means depending on rig-tungstenite directly with
   `default-features = false`. Both the manifest comment and MIGRATING.md say
   so now, instead of claiming a native-tls-only facade build. A build that
   silently cannot speak `wss://` is worse than one that compiles a TLS stack
   it does not use.

2. Erasing the connection un-`Sync`'d every session: `WebSocketConnection`'s
   only auto-trait supertrait was `WasmCompatSend`, so a session holding one
   boxed stopped being `Sync` — an undocumented break for hosts embedding a
   session in a `Sync` type. The trait requires `WasmCompatSync` now (every
   method takes `&mut self`, so no backend loses anything), and a
   `const _: fn()` probe asserts `Send + Sync` on the session and its builder
   so it cannot regress silently.

3. The cancelled-read pushback only restored a *frame*: a buffered `Err` whose
   caller had gone away was dropped, and the failure resurfaced later as a bare
   "connection closed before the turn finished" instead of the real cause. It
   pushes back errors too.

4. rig-tungstenite's wasm `compile_error!` was drowned by 17 follow-on errors,
   because the module declarations and crate-root imports were ungated. They
   are gated now, and `check-tungstenite-native-only` asserts exactly one error
   on wasm, mirroring `check-rmcp-native-only`.

5. Restored the error-space coverage the move had quietly dropped, and which
   the cassette matrix's doc still claimed: the 2xx/3xx rejection statuses
   (tungstenite raises `Error::Http` for any non-101 response, and
   `connect_async` does not follow redirects) and the exhaustive enumeration of
   every non-`Http` tungstenite variant, now in rig-tungstenite where that half
   of the mapping lives. The doc points at both halves and the end-to-end test
   that joins them.

* fix: keep the websocket contract reachable on wasm, cap the read-ahead, and four review fixes

Third review pass on #2426.

1. The facade's `websocket` feature pulled `rig-tungstenite` unconditionally,
   and that crate raises a native-only `compile_error!` on wasm — so enabling
   `websocket` for a wasm target failed the build, and the escape hatch that
   error itself prescribes (implement `ws_client::WebSocketClientExt` over
   `web_sys::WebSocket`) was unreachable through the facade. That undercut the
   whole point of moving the contract into rig-core.

   The backend is now a `cfg(not(target_family = "wasm"))` dependency, so
   `websocket` means "the protocol, plus the bundled backend where one exists":
   on wasm it degrades to `rig-core/websocket` alone and `rig::ws_client` stays
   reachable. All three websocket selectors now build for both targets, and
   `rig-tungstenite` named directly on wasm still gives exactly one error.

2. The actor's inbound buffer was unbounded: reading continuously is what makes
   a cancelled read safe and keeps tungstenite's pongs flowing, but a host that
   reads slowly could accumulate an entire streamed response in memory while
   TCP kept delivering. It stops draining the socket past `READ_AHEAD`, which
   restores the backpressure the pre-split code got for free.

3. `tracing` was declared and never used; `bytes` and `http` were normal
   dependencies used only in tests. All three landed in every downstream build
   of the new crate.

4. The connect-timeout message changed when the deadline moved to the backend.
   Documented in MIGRATING.md and pinned by a test, since it is what a host
   sees on a hung handshake.

5. Two stale doc comments: the scripted connection releases a turn per write
   (nothing is released on connect), and `WEBSOCKET_EXEMPTIONS` had been
   inserted between `expected_aliases`'s doc comment and the function.

refactor: generate the provider alias tree from rig-core's rustdoc output (#2427)

* refactor: generate the provider alias tree from rig-core's rustdoc output

`crates/rig-reqwest/src/providers.rs` is 333 lines of aliases whose own module
doc claimed it was "Generated from the provider sources". No generator existed:
it was typed by hand, and `tests/providers_complete.rs` only checked it by
string-scanning both the rig-core sources and the alias file itself.

That checker failed open. It matched the literal prefixes `pub type ` /
`pub struct ` followed by exactly `<H>` or `<T>`, so a `pub struct Foo<H =
Missing>` or a rustfmt-wrapped generic list was invisible; it derived the
provider module from the first path component only; it carried a hardcoded
`["minimax","moonshot","xiaomimimo","zai"]` fixup plus a second special case for
`impl_model_lister!`, because macro-generated types appear in no source line;
and it re-implemented a second parser for the alias file, so the two halves
could disagree about what a type name is.

`cargo xtask generate-provider-aliases` replaces both. The source of truth is
rig-core's own rustdoc JSON, which answers the question the text scan could
only approximate:

- macro-generated types are ordinary items there, so the fixups are gone;
- the transport parameter is reported with its default, so
  `ClientBuilder<H = Missing>` — which deliberately starts with an empty
  transport slot — is left alone, and the parameter's *name* (`H` in most
  providers, `T` in voyageai and azure) stops mattering;
- the `audio` and `image` gates are derived by building the surface once per
  feature instead of being restated in the generator;
- the websocket exemption added in #2426 is derived too: rig-reqwest does not
  enable rig-core's `websocket` feature, so those types are not in the surface.

Two things the JSON does not hand over, and how they are handled:

- rustdoc reports an item's *definition* path, which may run through a private
  module (`azure::audio_generation` is private and re-exported), so the
  generator walks the public module tree — following both re-export kinds — and
  aliases the shortest publicly nameable path.
- A payload envelope like `ApiResponse<T>` satisfies "one parameter, no default"
  while its parameter is a response body, not a transport. `NOT_A_TRANSPORT` is
  the one hand-maintained list left, three entries with reasons, and a stale
  entry fails generation rather than rotting.

The generated tree contains exactly the same 114 aliases as the hand-written
one, and `cargo public-api` reports rig-reqwest's public API byte-identical to
main, so this is a no-op for callers.

`--check` is what makes a MISSING alias fail CI, which the compiler cannot do:
it catches an alias naming a type that does not exist, never a type with no
alias. New CI job `check-provider-aliases` runs it on the pinned stable
toolchain (`RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1`; the format version is pinned so a toolchain bump
fails loudly instead of generating a wrong tree).

* ci: give the alias-tree job rustfmt, and say so when it is missing

The new `check-provider-aliases` job failed on its first run: the generator
formats its output with rustfmt so the committed file is `cargo fmt --check`
clean, and the rust-setup action deliberately installs only the components a
job asks for. It asks for rustfmt now.

The failure also read as "rustfmt rejected the generated source", which is the
wrong diagnosis for a component that is not installed — the task now names the
setup fix on both the spawn and the non-zero-exit path.

refactor!: rig-reqwest API and hygiene cleanups (#2428)

Phase 3 of the rig-reqwest review, after #2426 (websockets) and #2427 (the
generated alias tree). Eight independent items.

**The transport newtypes expose their inner client once, not three ways.**
`ReqwestClient` and `ReqwestMiddlewareClient` each had a public tuple field, a
`Deref`, and a `From`. `Deref` on a type that is not a smart pointer makes
reqwest's whole inherent API look like the newtype's own; the public field made
it redundant besides. Both now have a private field, `new`, `into_inner` and
`AsRef`. `ReqwestMiddlewareClient` gains the erasure `ReqwestClient` already had
(`boxed()`, `From<…> for BoxedHttpClient`) — a host that erases its transport
should not lose the option by having chosen middleware — and deliberately still
has no `Default`, since a middleware client with no middleware is a
`reqwest::Client` with extra indirection.

**`multipart_form` reports an unusable content type instead of dropping it.**
It rebuilt the part without its content type and sent the request anyway, so a
provider saw a part with no content type and answered about the wrong problem.
It returns `Result` now. Rig's parts carry a parsed `mime::Mime`, so this fires
only on a `mime`/`reqwest` version skew — the point is that it fires at all.
New `tests/multipart.rs` asserts the content type, filename and text parts reach
the wire, against a socket: reqwest's `Form` cannot be read back, so nothing
was covering the property that actually matters to a provider.

**rig-milvus no longer duplicates `from_reqwest`.** It had a byte-identical
copy. It holds a `reqwest::Client` directly rather than an `H: HttpClientExt`,
so depending on rig-reqwest is not a layering violation — and with
`default-features = false` the dependency count went *down* (207 → 167), since
the crate was already carrying rig-reqwest as a dev-dependency with default
features on.

**`into_lazy_response` and `into_eager_response` were one line apart.** They are
one function taking a `BodyTiming` now, and the three cfg-selected bindings that
chose between them collapse into one `OFF_RUNTIME_TIMING` constant.

**`RuntimeUnavailable` was `pub` in a private module**, so unnameable by

refactor!: remove every backwards-compatibility shim (#2429)

caller or an older persisted record kept working.

  `CompletionRequestBuilder::without_preamble`. The builder has always
  emitted the preamble as the leading `Message::System` of `chat_history`
  and left the field `None`, yet every provider still read it, so a
  hand-built request could carry a second system prompt through a path the
  builder never used. `CompletionRequest::system_instructions()` (the leading
  system message's text) replaces the reads. Telemetry
  `gen_ai.system_instructions` was populated from the always-`None` field
  and therefore never recorded anything; it now records the leading system
  message.
- The `#[deprecated]` retired model constants in deepseek, cohere and
  mistral are deleted.
- `rig_candle::{LlamaModel, ModelFamily}` aliases are deleted; internal
  uses renamed to `CandleModel` / `ConversationProtocol`.
- Persisted-record tolerances are deleted: `CompletionCall::usage` no longer
  accepts `null`, OpenAI `UserContent::Audio` no longer accepts the
  never-on-the-wire `"audio"` tag, and OpenAI `ToolResultContent` derives
  its `type`-tagged decoder instead of tolerating a missing tag.

Tests that existed only to pin a removed tolerance are deleted; the two that
also covered live behaviour (suspended-run resume, OpenAI message decoding)
are rewritten to the current shapes. No cassette changed: the preamble path
was funnel-equivalent, so request bodies are byte-identical.

refactor: bound hygiene — raw Send/Sync in wasm-built code becomes precise (#2430)

Ownership/lifetimes/bounds audit, theme 1. Every raw `Send`/`Sync` bound in
wasm-compiled code either becomes the `WasmCompat*` form, gains its missing
wasm sibling, or disappears because a supertrait already provides it. On
native targets every signature is equivalent (`WasmCompatSend: Send` with a
blanket impl); on browser wasm the changed signatures are strict relaxations.

- ollama, hyperbolic, huggingface/gemini image generation: inherent-impl
  `T: HttpClientExt + Clone + Send + 'static` -> `WasmCompatSend`, matching
  the shared internal image-generation helper these predate.
- ImageGenerationError / AudioGenerationError: `RequestError` gains the
  `#[cfg(target_family = "wasm")]` non-Send sibling that TranscriptionError,
  CompletionError and VectorStoreError already have.
- InMemoryVectorIndex's VectorStoreIndex impl and EmbeddingsBuilder's build
  impl: raw `Send`/`Sync` -> markers (the traits they implement already use
  them; `buffer_unordered` needs no `Send`).
- DeviceCodeHandler: the stored callback is `dyn Fn + Send + Sync` only where
  the markers mean Send/Sync (browser wasm ignores the handler entirely), via
  a cfg-paired `DeviceCodeCallback` alias; `new`/`on_device_code` bounds use
  the markers.
- rig-agent retrieval indexes: `Arc<dyn VectorStoreIndexDyn + Send + Sync>`
  and `impl VectorStoreIndexDyn + Send + Sync + 'static` drop the auto-trait
  bounds outright — `VectorStoreIndexDyn`'s `WasmCompat*` supertraits already
  provide them on native and correctly nothing on browser wasm.

Sites read and deliberately left alone: the already-cfg-paired boxed-error
enums and stream aliases, native-only compile-time asserts, `#[cfg(test)]`
compile-coverage modules, tokio spawn bounds in rig-reqwest/rig-tungstenite
runtimes, and every crate outside the CI wasm matrix.
