* fix(agent)!: whoever is awaiting drives — no run owns the driver

The agent's driver sat behind a mutex whose guard a run took on its first
pending poll and released only in `Drop`. A stream its owner had drained
but kept in scope, two streams polled alternately, or a `prompt()` awaited
inside a `while let` over a stream all left the guard with a run nobody
polled — every other run on the agent then waited on a lock for a driver
that never advanced. That was a hang reachable through the public API,
which the ownership rule promised was impossible.

`Driven` no longer holds the driver: it takes the lock only for one
synchronous poll, and the driver is polled with a waker built from a
bus-wide set of every live run's waker, so progress inside the driver (a
provider reply, a timer, a queued command) wakes whichever run is awaiting
it, even after the run that last polled has finished or been dropped. A
run polled from inside another run's driver poll (a tool that runs a
nested prompt on a clone) finds the lock taken and simply yields — the
poll in progress serves its dispatches too. A finished run unregisters
its waker; a dropped run still gives the driver one last poll so its
abandoned dispatches are observed as cancelled immediately — with the
bus-wide waker, never a noop one, so the runs still live keep being woken.

another run; two streams polled alternately; a prompt awaited inside a
stream loop on a clone; a run dropped mid-tool cancels the tool at once;
a nested agent call from inside a tool is served by the driving run.

* fix(core)!: command_capacity bounds the bus, not each sender

The command channel was a `futures::channel::mpsc` and every dispatch
cloned the sender. That channel grants each `Sender` clone one guaranteed
slot, so no dispatch ever parked at its send stage: `command_capacity`
bounded nothing, the "pressure lands on the pending" contract was
vacuous, and Bevy proof 5 passed without proving it.

The buffer is now one bounded queue on the bus's shared half. A dispatch
whose first poll finds it full keeps its command and parks its waker; the
driver's drain wakes every parked dispatch, and the next poll of each
sends. Dropping a parked `Pending`/`EffectStream` sends nothing. The driver
ends when the last `Dispatcher` clone drops (a refcount replaces the
sender count) with nothing buffered or in flight, and dropping the driver
fails every command it never took with `BusClosed` — the buffer outlives
the driver now, so the driver's drop guard drains it.

`Dispatcher::buffered()` exposes the buffer depth (at most the bound);
the capacity test asserts the bound holds across eighteen parked
dispatches, a parked dispatch sends after a drain, a dispatch dropped
while parked never reaches its handler, and a buffered dispatch answers
`BusClosed` when the driver drops first. Bevy proof 5 asserts the same
bound. Micro-bench: unary dispatch median 2.75 µs (p90 2.83 µs), down
from 2.9 µs — one lock replaces a channel clone per dispatch.

* fix(core)!: a serial key never strands its queue, and never waits on itself

Two ways a dispatch could wait forever under `serial_per_handler: true`
while the bus was alive:

- `serve` answered a command whose handler was gone with
  `HandlerUnavailable` and returned without marking the key busy or
  looking further, and `release` popped exactly one queued command per
  completion. Deregister a key with A in flight and B, C queued: A's
  completion popped B (failed on the spot), and C sat in the queue with
  nothing left in flight to ever release it. `serve` now reports whether
  the command went in flight, `release` keeps popping until one does or
  the queue is empty, and deregistration wakes the driver, which drains
  every queue whose handler is gone with `HandlerUnavailable`.

- A handler that dispatched to its own key from inside its own poll (a
  tool running a nested prompt whose model calls that same tool) queued
  behind the very command that was waiting on it. The driver now records
  which key it is synchronously polling, on which thread; a dispatch to
  that key made during that poll on that thread is the handler's own and
  is refused with a `Request` report naming the key, instead of hung.
  Concurrent serving is unaffected: a nested dispatch to the same key is
  served alongside.

Pinned: deregistering a serial key drains B and C with the key in the
message while A completes and a re-registered key serves again; the
re-entrant dispatch is refused under serial serving and accepted under
concurrent serving; at the agent level, a nested run whose model calls
the tool in flight completes with the nested call skipped.

* fix(core)!: one retry table

Two tables answered "is this retryable" and disagreed. `ErrorReport`'s
tool row hardcoded `Timeout | RateLimited | Network | Provider`, while
`ToolErrorKind`'s own `kind_defaults!` table says `Provider => None`: a
`Provider` tool error reported `retryable() == None` on one side and
`is_retryable() == true` on the other, and the wire carried the second.
And `retryable_status(None) == true` marked every response-less failure
retryable — a malformed header value, a missing header set, an unexpected
content type — as if "no status" meant "the request never reached a
decision".

Now `ToolErrorKind::default_retryable` (the `kind_defaults!` table, made
public) is the one source: `retryable()`, `is_retryable()` and the wire
report agree for every kind, and a kind that leaves it to the tool
(`None`) is not retryable on the wire (ruled: the wire field is a bool;
a caller that wants "unknown" reads the kind). `retryable_status(None)`
is `false`; a status-less failure is classified by what it is, in
`transient_transport`: transient when the request never reached a
decision (`StreamEnded`, the backend's own `Instance` errors — connect
resets, DNS, TLS, timeouts) and permanent when the client could not form
the request or read the response (`Protocol`, `InvalidHeaderValue`,
`NoHeaders`, `InvalidContentType`); a status-carrying transport failure
follows the status table, and a provider response without a status
decides nothing.

Pinned: the per-status table with `None => false`; the per-variant
transport table; every tool kind answering the same on all three
surfaces, with the override winning.

* feat(core)!: ToolContext keys are declared, not derived

A context slot was keyed by `std::any::type_name::<T>()`: documented as
unstable across compiler versions, and changed by any rename or module
move. A persisted `EffectLog` (or a record written by another toolchain)
replayed after a refactor read every context value as missing —
silently: `get` swallowed a decode failure as `None`, and rmcp's `Meta`
forwarding then sent no `_meta` at all.

(`#[derive(ContextValue)]`, key defaulting to the type's name,

accessor is bound on it; the key is the value's identity on the wire.
`get`/`result`/`remove` return `Result<Option<T>, ToolContextError>`: an
empty slot is `Ok(None)`, a slot holding something that is not a `T` is
`Err(Decode)` — absence and a shape mismatch are different facts.
`insert` never fails after a successful write: a displaced value that
does not decode as `T` is replaced, not a reason to unwind the caller.
Error messages name the declared key.

Foreign types cannot implement the trait (orphan rule), so rig-rmcp's
MCP values are newtypes with fixed keys: `McpMeta` (`rmcp.meta`, the
request `_meta` a caller places inbound), and on the result map
`McpStructuredContent`, `McpResponseMeta`, `McpCallToolResult`. The A2
census gains its key column; the in-tree value types (`SessionId`,
`MockRequestId`, `FailureSite`, the doc examples' `AuditRecord`) declare
theirs. Pinned: the derive's default and overridden keys and the JSON
the context serializes to; `get` reporting `Decode` for a slot of a
different shape; `insert` returning `Ok(None)` over an undecodable
displaced value. Every context test converts to declared newtypes with
its assertions' meaning kept.

* fix(bus): a dispatch cancelled before it is served is never served

A `Pending` or `EffectStream` dropped between its send and the driver's
next poll — a Bevy entity despawned in the frame it dispatched — was
still served for one poll: `serve` built the handler future and
`select(serving, cancel)` polled the handler before it saw the already
resolved cancel. One poll of a provider call is an HTTP request, and
`recorder.begin` had opened a record nobody wanted, later resolved as
"the handler dropped its outcome sink".

`serve` now checks the cancel signal before touching the handler table:
a command whose consumer is gone is dropped unserved — no handler poll,
no record, no serial slot. The in-flight race keeps its order on
purpose: a handler already running observes the cancel on its own next
poll (`SinkClosed`) before its future is dropped, which is how a
streaming adapter stops cleanly (the stream-cancel test and fixture
proof 6 pin that contract).

a counting recorder, a serial key not left busy by a cancelled command,

against the previous driver: a cancelled dispatch was recorded as a
handler failure), and the Bevy fixture's proof 4 gains the buffered
variant.

* fix(core): a cancelled dispatch is recorded as cancelled

The sink's `Drop` reported every unanswered dispatch the same way —
`Internal "the handler dropped its outcome sink without answering"` for
a unary one, the truncation report for a stream — whether the handler
had failed to answer or the driver had dropped the handler future
because the consumer dropped its `Pending`/`EffectStream`. A log of a
cancelled run therefore replayed the cancel as a handler failure, and a
durable-execution resume through that log could not tell the two apart.

The sink knows the difference at drop time: when the reply half is
already closed (`is_closed()`), the consumer is gone, and the record now
says `ErrorKind::Cancelled` (`rig_core::serve::cancelled()`), never
retryable. A handler that returned without answering while the
consumer is still waiting keeps the `Internal`/truncation report.

Also: `OutcomeSink::send` checks a finished stream sink before tapping
the item, so the tap sees only what the consumer could receive (the
order was wrong; the path is unreachable today because `resolve`
consumes the sink, so no test can pin it — recorded).

flight are recorded as `Cancelled`, and a replayer registered from that

* feat(bus)!: hosts probe pendings; one waker per parked sender

A host that ticks rather than awaits — a Bevy system, once per frame —
had only `block_on(poll_once(&mut pending))`, which mints a fresh waker
per frame; a `Pending` parked on a full buffer pushed that waker into
the bus's parked-sender list every frame (`will_wake` never matched a
fresh one), so a stalled driver — a serial key on a slow provider —
meant a per-frame leak for as long as the stall lasted.

`Pending::poll_outcome` and `EffectStream::poll_item` are the probe: one
poll under a no-op waker, no executor, `None` until ready. A parked
value now owns one `AtomicWaker` slot in the bus's list, registered
once and re-armed with the latest waker per poll, so ten thousand
probes (or ten thousand real wakers) hold one slot, and the drain and
the close skip slots whose value was dropped. `Future`/`Stream` polling
is unchanged and the two may be mixed (the bus keeps the latest waker).

The `Send` assertions for `Pending`, `EffectStream`, `ModelHandle` and
`Dispatcher` are no longer native-only: they hold serde data, channels
and atomics on every target, and a Bevy `Component` in the browser
needs the guarantee there. `BusDriver: Send` stays native-only, as it
must. Budgets: `Pending` 48 → 56, `EffectStream` 144 → 152 (one `Arc`);
the budgets themselves are unchanged. Bench unchanged.

Tests: a probe resolves a unary and a stream dispatch without an
executor; ten thousand probes and ten thousand fresh wakers on a full
bus keep one slot; a parked value dropped before the drain leaves no
slot. The Bevy fixture's proof 3 probes with `poll_outcome` (proof 7
keeps `block_on(poll_once)`), and proof 6 holds its `EffectStream` in a
component, probes it per tick and cancels by despawn.

* feat(core)!: the external-resolver seam — a sink can leave its handler

A tool that is a Bevy system, an approval gate, a human at a console:
anything that answers an effect outside the handler's own future. The
sink was already `Send + Sync` data and could be moved out of a `Serve`
impl, but the driver keyed the dispatch's lifetime on the *handler
future*: it released the serial slot, decremented `in_flight` and
closed the recorder's view when the future returned, so a system-
resolved key under `serial_per_handler` was served twice concurrently
and the log's order was not the serve order.

`OutcomeSink::detach(self) -> DetachedSink` is the seam: a handler
detaches, hands the sink to whoever will answer, and returns. The sink
now carries a `done` sender (`OutcomeSink::with_done`, part of the
driver seam) that drops when it answers or is dropped; the driver's
`Serving` task completes only when both the handler future has ended
*and* that receiver has resolved, so a detached dispatch keeps its
slot, its count and its record until the resolver answers.
Cancellation reaches the resolver through `DetachedSink::is_closed`.
`OutcomeSink` and `DetachedSink` are asserted `Send + Sync + 'static`.

Deviation from the prompt, recorded: the constructors `unary`/`stream`
keep their signatures and the driver adds the sender with `with_done`
(the inline path and the writer tests build sinks without one).

Finding: the handler future had to be dropped *before* awaiting the
sink's receiver — the future owns the sink until then, and awaiting
with it alive is a deadlock (the old `pin_mut!` kept it on the task's
stack past the select). Also documents, on `serial_per_handler`, the
nested dispatch the bus cannot detect (one made from another task).

* feat(bus): a driver is re-created over a live dispatcher

`Drop for BusDriver` closed the `Shared` every `Dispatcher`, `Handle<F>`
and `Registrar` point at, permanently: a plugin whose driver task was
cancelled on a state transition, or whose entity was despawned, had
every handle in its world turn into a dead value that had to be re-bound
and re-inserted everywhere. Proof 4 proved the death; nothing proved a
way back.

`Bus::reopen(&Dispatcher) -> Result<(Registrar, BusDriver), _>` is the
way back: it succeeds when no driver is alive (`Request`, retryable,
otherwise — a cancelled task is dropped by its executor on its own
time, so a host retries next tick), clears the close, and returns a
fresh driver over the same `Shared` with the bus's config. Handlers
died with the old driver, so the descriptor table is cleared on driver
drop (it described nothing; `descriptor()`/`handle::<F>()` no longer
answer for ghosts) and the caller re-registers. Nothing in flight is
resurrected: a `Pending`/`EffectStream` remembers the bus generation it
was minted under and answers `BusClosed` after a restart whether it was
sent or not, including one whose reply was lost with the old driver
(`reply_dropped` checks the generation, not only the close). A handle
bound before the restart works after it: a handle is a key over the
bus, not over a driver.

`Shared::new` takes the `BusConfig` (a reopened driver keeps it).
Budget: `Typed<Completion>` 64 → 80 (a `Pending` grew by its generation
and its parked slot); `Pending` and `EffectStream` sit exactly at 64
and 160.

* fix(agent): every error ending settles once, before its error reaches the consumer

fix(gemini, rig-ecs): retry transient provider failures inside the run; block_reason=OTHER is not a refusal (#2500)

* fix(gemini): a prompt blocked for OTHER or an unknown reason is transient, not a refusal

SAFETY, BLOCKLIST and PROHIBITED_CONTENT judge the prompt's content and
stay a final ProviderError. OTHER is Google's "blocked due to unknown
reasons": the same prompt is answered on the next call, as two of three
dev-tier attempts of one rigcoder task showed. It and any block reason
this crate does not know travel as a ProviderResponse without a status,
carrying the reason as the code and the transport's transient verdict,
so is_retryable and the ErrorReport say so without any caller reading
the message. Both wires classify alike; one test per reason on each.

* feat(rig-ecs): retry a completion lost to a retryable provider failure inside the run

A completion whose outcome is a provider report with retryable set is
re-issued over the same history while ProviderRetried < ProviderRetries
(the run's, else the agent's, else 3): the lost turn is read and leaves
no utterance, the run wants a turn again under ProviderRetrying, and
Advance spawns it without checking or spending MaxTurns. No tool is
re-run, no history is rewritten, every attempt is its own effect in the
log and replays in order. A non-retryable report, a cancellation or a
spent budget ends the run Failed(Provider) as before. The witness gets
rig-ecs/agent/provider_retry (attempt, budget, reason).

Time is the host's: the library issues the retry on the next pass; a
backoff is a hold a Gate system acquires on the re-issued effect and
releases when due, so wasm builds and replay need no clock. The budget
joins the policy identity (spec_json provider_retries); the three
components are in scenes and the reflect registry.

* fix(openai): decode echoed Responses metadata leniently (#2483, #2493)

The response wire struct reached the request-shaped AdditionalParameters
through #[serde(flatten)], so one optional metadata field disagreeing
with its Rust type discarded the whole response: MiniMax-style endpoints
echo top_p as an object (#2483), and with serde_json/arbitrary_precision
enabled anywhere in the graph even top_p: 0.95 failed because the flatten
buffer skips numeric coercion, turning the response.completed frame that
carries usage into a hard stream error (#2493).

existing Responses cassette replays without fixture edits. A new
response_metadata_matrix cassette suite records the numeric shape live
and derives object-shaped siblings from those recordings.

* fix(rig-postgres): filtered and thresholded searches generate valid SQL (#2376)

Four rendering bugs made any VectorSearchRequest with a member filter, a
single-condition filter, or a threshold fail in Postgres: `is in` is not
an operator; `WHERE` had no separator; the threshold named the
`distance` select-list alias inside the inner SELECT's WHERE; and it
compared a distance with > although threshold is a minimum similarity.

Render IN, separate WHERE, and apply the threshold as
score_expression >= $n per distance operator (the approach rig-sqlite
uses). Returned scores stay raw ascending distances, so callers without a
threshold see no change. DB-free unit tests pin the rendered SQL; the
Docker-backed integration test gains a filtered + thresholded cell.

* feat(core): the wire model's shared surface — Wire, Operation, Decoder, framers, one driver

wire.rs, http_client/framing.rs, operation/, driver.rs: what a provider is
(data plus an encoder and a decoder), what an operation is, and the one
driver that pushes bytes between them. Unary is a stream of one frame: call
frames a whole body with the same framer and drives it through the same
decoder a stream would, so the two paths cannot drift.

* feat(core): encode takes the mode

A wire that asks for a streamed reply sends a different request — the chat
wires set stream: true, Gemini switches endpoint and adds ?alt=sse — and
recorded traffic pins those bytes. The decoder is the same either way.

* feat(xtask): check-wires — inside rig-core's providers, everything is a wire

No .await, no async, no transport type parameter, no consumer-trait impl,
and nothing shared, erased or deferred inside an impl Wire block. Parsed
with syn, so an .await in a doc comment cannot trip it. The websocket
session is the one exception: one connection and many turns is not a
request/response exchange. In the verify plan's tooling check.

* feat(anthropic): the Messages wire, and the unary reply as one more frame

Anthropic becomes data: one config struct, three wires (Messages, Models,
Verify) and five dialect constants. The unary reply is a "message" frame
whose interpret synthesizes the stream it would have been, so there is no
second Content -> AssistantContent mapping and no normalize; the block code
that assembles a streamed turn is the only code that assembles a buffered
one.

Also lands the two shared-surface additions the embedding slices needed:
Operation::fold seeds a fold from the request (an embedding response joins
the provider's vectors back onto its own input), and Encoded::batch lets a
provider that takes one item per request answer a batch in order.

* feat(providers): openai chat, openai responses, gemini, cohere, ollama, voyageai as wires

Every HTTP provider in rig-core now has a data config, one wire per
operation, and one decoder serving both its unary and its streamed replies.
Adds classify_or so a wire with more than one reply shape composes its
classifiers instead of reading a verdict itself.

* test(core): the driver is the policy home

WireDriver is where the frame-triage table lives now, so driver.rs and the
trait definitions in wire.rs join adapter.rs and the classify layer as the
files allowed to name the triage variants. The driver's capture of a unary
reply body as CompletionResponse::raw is allowlisted with its reason: it is
the provider's own reply, not a frame decode.

* refactor(core): run_wire_stream is the async wrapper over the shared fold

The wrapper is bounded on Decoder<Completion, F> rather than WireAdapter, so
a typed transport — an AWS event stream, a gRPC stream, an in-process
generator — reuses the driver's policy without an HTTP request behind it.
Adds Bind (blanket) in rig-core and DefaultTransport::bound in rig-reqwest:
rig-core depends on no transport, so the crate that owns one supplies the
default socket.

* test(core): the scripted fold double speaks the operation-generic decoder

* feat(core): one seam for building a completion model, and three named non-wire surfaces

CompletionProvider is what the six *Client traits were for, reduced to the
one thing a caller wanted: Bound<P, H> satisfies it for every wire-backed
provider, and the typed transports implement it directly because their
frames are an SDK's types rather than bytes. check-wires now enumerates the
three surfaces a pure encode structurally cannot be — a connection (the
Responses websocket), a conversation (credential exchange), and a resource
lifecycle (Gemini's cached content) — so a fourth cannot appear unseen.

* feat(core): copilot, gemini sessions, dialect fixes, and the caller migration in flight

* fix(core): raw is the reply document on every path, not a summary of it

A unary call over the Responses wire on a dialect that always streams gets
an event stream for an answer, so there are no bytes for the driver to
parse as the reply document. Decoder::document lets the decoder hand back
the envelope its terminal event carried, and the driver prefers the reply's
own bytes, then that. The streamed fold carries the terminal record's raw
for the same reason: the escape hatch must not depend on whether the caller
streamed.

fix: publish the facade, not the repository — and stop asking for dependencies nothing uses (#2563)

* fix(rig): allowlist what the facade publishes

Fixes #2349.

The root manifest is both the workspace root and the `rig` facade
package, so the package directory is the whole repository and
`cargo package` sweeps it. The facade's own library is one file of
re-exports; everything else in the tarball was inherited from the
directory layout: CI workflows and issue templates, README artwork the
README never references, the Nix flake, release tooling,
`examples/documents/deepseek_r1.pdf`, and a 1.3 MiB `tests/` tree
carrying a 741 KiB JPEG and an MP3.

That test tree cannot compile from the tarball under any circumstances:
thirteen of its files use `rig-test-support`, a path-only dev dependency
Cargo strips when publishing.

#2349 asked for an allowlist rather than an exclude list, and measured
why: cargo packages untracked-but-unignored files, so an exclude list
still ships whatever a maintainer happens to have lying next to the
manifest at publish time. Reproduced on the parent commit - an untracked
`scratch-stray-note.md` in the root appears in `cargo package --list`.
With `include` it does not.

174 files and 4.13 MiB become 13 files and 417 KiB compressed. The four
images the README displays stay, because a registry renders that README
out of the tarball; the five it never mentions go.

The second half of #2349 was a CI gate, since a manifest key states
intent once and only CI re-checks it - and a gate also catches the one
failure mode an allowlist introduces, a needed file left out.
`cargo xtask check-packaging` asserts the facade's file list and holds
every publishable crate under 8 MiB uncompressed, well inside
crates.io's 10 MiB compressed cap that 0.41.0 came within 4.9% of. The
`tooling` check runs it, and any manifest or `xtask/` change already
selects that check.

The check only ever runs `cargo package --list`, never `--no-verify`:
`cargo package` builds the tarball's lockfile from the published
manifest even with `--no-verify`, resolving each sibling `rig-*` against
crates.io. On a release PR that version is not published yet, so the
check could not go green until the version published and the version
could not publish until the check went green. `--list` is immune, at the
cost of measuring uncompressed bytes - which is the safe direction,
since compressed is never larger.

Packaging now emits a `warning: ignoring test` line per test target, as
`rig-core` and `rig-cassette` already do. These are deliberately not
silenced with `autotests = false`, which would stop local discovery too
and recreate the "tests run in no CI job" hole behind #2258.

Finding PC01.

* fix(deps): stop declaring dependencies no crate source uses

Every `[dependencies]` entry is resolved, built and carried in each
consumer's supply chain whether or not the crate's own code names it.
Fourteen entries across eleven published crates were named by nothing
under `src/` or `build.rs`.

The one with real weight is `rig-bedrock`: it declared `rig-derive` as a
normal dependency for the sake of two examples, so every consumer of the
`bedrock` facade feature built the proc-macro crate and the
`proc-macro-crate` behind it in order to link a library that expands no
derive at all. `rig-gemini-grpc` and `rig-scylladb` did the same with
`tracing`, and `rig-fastembed` with `serde`; those move to
`[dev-dependencies]`, where their tests and examples still find them.
The remaining ten are deleted outright.

Each entry was confirmed by removing it and rebuilding the crate: the
library alone for the verdict, then `--workspace --all-targets`, because
feature unification across the workspace can satisfy an example's
`required-features` and reveal a use a per-crate build hides. That
second pass is what caught `rig-fastembed`'s `serde`, which a per-crate
check had wrongly cleared for deletion.

`cargo xtask check-packaging` now fails on a dependency no checked-in
source names, with one documented exemption: `rig-gemini-grpc`'s
`tonic-prost` is named only by the service code its build script writes
into `OUT_DIR`, which is not on disk to scan.

Finding PC02.

* test(facade): put every facade feature inside the additivity guard

`tests/fixtures/tool_facade` is where the root's features are proved
additive: its `--all-features` row turns on `all_root`, which lists the
facade features to compile together. `typesafeai` was never added to
that list, so the one guard that builds every `rig` feature at once
skipped it and a break in its forwarding would have reached a release
unobserved.

Adding it compiles clean, so this closes a coverage gap rather than a
live break. `cargo xtask check-packaging` now compares `all_root`
against the root manifest's own feature table, so the next feature
added to the facade cannot quietly stay outside the guard; `default`
and `facade-build-tests` are exempt, since the guard's other rows
already build the first and the second only selects the guard itself.

Finding PC04.

Reasoning now records the service that issued it (`Reasoning::provider`),
stamped when a completion is decoded, streamed or folded from a stream. A
request drops reasoning another service issued before it is encoded
(`message::retain_replayable_reasoning`): the shared driver, Bedrock,
gemini-grpc and Vertex AI all scope history this way. Reasoning of unknown
provenance, including histories serialized before this change, is replayed
as before. Claude on Bedrock records `anthropic`, since Anthropic documents
thinking signatures as valid across the Claude API, Bedrock and Google
Cloud; gemini-grpc records the Gemini API service it shares with REST.

Also:
- fix(bedrock): name documents by content hash with an occurrence suffix
  instead of a random uuid, so requests are deterministic and unique names
  survive repeated content.
- fix(anthropic): usage observations carry `thinking_tokens`.
- feat(telemetry): completion spans record the transport request id as
  `rig.provider_request_id` on success and on provider errors.

* test(cassette): exact-slot survival oracle and stateful handle round-trip cells

The history-survival oracle now requires each delivered value in the slot
that must carry it, anchored to its owner (call, thinking block, Gemini part
kind, encrypted item), and counts legacy placeholders without judging them.
New recorded cells cover OpenAI stored and stateless Responses chains and
file ids, Gemini cachedContents and Interactions chains with cleanup,
reasoning across serde, ECS checkpoint restore and agent memory, generated
images fed back as input, request-id identity on every surface, and
adversarial histories. Portability rows are re-recorded after the provenance
fix and assert no foreign reasoning is forwarded.

* test(cassette): tighten file chain assertions

feat(core)!: signature slots, upstream reasoning provenance and the legacy fixture corpus (#2580)

* feat(gemini)!: keep answer-text thought signatures on their own part

Gemini returns a thoughtSignature on the part that carried it, including
answer text parts. Rig moved a text part's signature onto a synthesized
reasoning block, so a continuation sent it back on a thought part.

Assistant `Text` now carries the signature in `additional_params` under
the wire's key (`gemini` for the Gemini API over REST and gRPC, `vertexai`
for Vertex AI), and each codec replays it on the text part. Text chunks
across stream events continue one part, a signed part ends it, and an
empty signed part stays its own part. The Vertex decoder previously
dropped these signatures. `attach_trailing_signature` is removed.

* feat(openrouter)!: attribute relayed reasoning to its upstream family

Reasoning received through OpenRouter recorded `openrouter` as its
issuer, so a conversation that switched upstream model family replayed
foreign reasoning. The chat and Responses decoders now stamp the upstream
family from the response model: `anthropic` for Claude, whose signatures
verify between OpenRouter and the Claude API in both directions, and
`openrouter/<vendor>` for every other family, whose state is bound to
OpenRouter's upstream account. A request replays the requested model's
family, legacy `openrouter` reasoning and unknown provenance; a router or
preset model, which names no family, replays every relayed family.

OpenRouter's Responses route also returns Claude reasoning with a
`signature` beside the item, which the Responses types dropped, so the
thinking never reached Claude again. Responses reasoning items now carry
an optional `signature`, kept on the reasoning text and replayed.

`Operation::scope_to_wire` and `retain_replayable_reasoning` take the
accepted issuers as a slice; `Wire::replay_issuers` supplies them, and
`Reasoning::replayable_to` accepts a family issuer ending in `/`.

* fix(groq): remove the unreleased compound model constants

Groq removed groq/compound and groq/compound-mini from the developer catalog; both ids now return model_not_found.

* test: pin signature slots and upstream reasoning issuers

refactor(rig-core)!: unify provider operation errors (#2582)

* refactor(rig-core)!: unify provider operation errors

* refactor(rig-core)!: replace per-operation provider errors with ProviderError

One error type, rig_core::error::ProviderError, now serves completion,
embedding, rerank, transcription, image and audio generation, verification,
model listing and Gemini context caching. Its variant is its
classification, and each variant maps to one ErrorKind.

Deleted: CompletionError, EmbeddingError, RerankError, TranscriptionError,
ImageGenerationError, AudioGenerationError, CachedContentError, VerifyError,
ModelListingError, the WireError trait, Operation::Error, wire::Error<W>,
and the provider_error_enum!, impl_provider_response_helpers!,
impl_wire_error! and impl_report_for_provider_error! macros with their
per-type ErrorReport tables. rig-typesafeai drops its own error type and
rig-bedrock its ProviderReply trait.

Verification reclassifies 401/403 at the consumer, and cached content
reclassifies 403/404 on an existing handle, as before; both now keep the
provider's reply. Model listing keeps its provider and path through an
Operation::with_route hook and a non-serialized route on the preserved reply.

* test(rig-core): pin ProviderError reports to the replaced enums

Every former variant whose report is unchanged is compared field by field, the serialized reply and observation boundary included, against the reports the replaced enums produced. The listed behavior changes are asserted on their own: response-shaped embedding faults report the decode boundary, CacheExpired and InvalidAuthentication keep the provider's reply, and request-building failures share one shape.

* fix(rig-typesafeai): drop the thiserror dependency its deleted error type used

* refactor(rig-core): export ProviderError from the prelude and update stale references

The rig-core prelude exported CompletionError and VerifyError; it now exports their replacement, as the rig-agent prelude does. The crate README and the serde policy allowlist named the deleted types, and a historical test comment was rewritten by the rename.

refactor(rig-core)!: standardize modality request builders and unify GenAI spans (#2583)

* refactor(rig-core)!: standardize modality request builders and unify GenAI spans

* refactor(rig-core)!: take required values in the modality request builders' constructors

TranscriptionRequestBuilder, ImageGenerationRequestBuilder and
AudioGenerationRequestBuilder drop their Missing/Provided typestate. Like
CompletionRequestBuilder, each takes its required values in the constructor
(`new(model, data)` or `from_file(model, path)`, `new(model, prompt)`,
`new(model, text, voice)`), so omitting one is still a compile error. Each
wraps the request it builds instead of mirroring its fields. The model-trait
conveniences take the same values.

`additional_params` has one meaning on every request builder, shared through
json_utils::merge_params: repeated calls merge and `None` clears. Image and
audio replaced on each call before, and transcription's additional_params_opt
is removed.

* refactor(rig-core)!: one GenAI operation enum and span builder for every operation

GenAiOperation replaces CompletionOperation and ModalityOperation, and
SpanBuilder replaces CompletionSpanBuilder and ModalitySpanBuilder. A
completion operation still adopts a conforming completion-parent span or
opens a rig::completions child; every other operation still opens a fresh
rig::modalities span. Every span keeps its name, target, fields and values.

SpanCombinator::record_response records a response's ID, model and usage,
and every recording site uses it: the completion and modality operations,
instrument_modality, and bedrock. instrument_modality is generic over the
operation and reuses its telemetry and record hooks, so
ModalityResponseTelemetry, its macro and record_response_metadata are
removed. An equivalence test pins every span against the ones the replaced
builders opened.

* test(rig-core): guard the span unification and document the merge rule

Review follow-ups. Debug assertions keep a completion span from being opened
for a modality operation and the reverse, now that one enum carries both.
The span equivalence test records each span's parent and covers a completion
span under an ordinary ambient span and the rerank and transcription
operations; its expected values were regenerated from the pre-change code.
A modality span under a near-miss completion parent neither warns nor
adopts. The builder docs state that parameters merge key by key for JSON
objects, and the builder tests use a scoped temp dir and pin single-call
additional_params.

feat(cassette)!: refuse account failures and stored state, keep failed attempts, and move recording tooling into xtask (#2587)

* feat(cassette): keep failed recordings, log created resources, refuse account failures and stored state

Record mode now writes a failed test's exchanges under attempt_root()
instead of dropping them, never over the fixture. A relay in front of the
recording proxy, and the direct recorder for unary and multipart requests,
append every created stored response, file, cache, interaction,
conversation and vector store to ledger.jsonl before the reply reaches the
test; ledger::clean_up deletes them outside any cassette and treats 404, or
Gemini's 403 "not found", as gone. The attempt root defaults to the target
directory the running binary was built in, where cargo xtask looks.

finish() refuses a recording holding an account failure (auth, rate limit,
quota, credit) that the cell did not declare, classified by
reply_account_failure from the error's type and code, then its message,
including a failure delivered inside a 2xx stream; and an OpenAI or xAI
Responses recording that stored a response the session never deleted.

Move the recording tooling #2580 kept outside the repository into
cargo xtask cassette: owner-test resolution listing every producer,
record-by-owning-test with an attempt ledger written before and after each
run, a cap of six, restore-on-failure from a snapshot taken just before
the run, cleanup on every exit path, a spend estimate with the failed-attempt floor, a token-bounded
fixture scan with literal checks of exported secrets, golden regeneration
that reverts header.deliveries-only churn, and the created-resource cleanup
pass (the cassette_tool example).

rig-test-support gains assert_matches_recorded_document, which compares a
live document with its fixture at every depth, by type on volatile keys when
recording, and the comparison_guard that finds exact volatile comparisons

Unit tests for the account classifier, the ledger and cleanup, the relay

checks that committed account failures are declared by their cells, that

refactor(rig-core)!: classify every request-building failure as a request error (#2586)

* refactor(rig-core)!: classify every request-building failure as a request error

* refactor(rig-core)!: return a request-building error type from Wire::encode

`Wire::encode` returns `EncodeError`, whose only conversion into
`ProviderError` yields `Request`, `Url`, or a typed request parameter
variant. Before, each wire picked a variant by hand, so the same failure to
build a request reported as `response` (decode boundary), `http`,
`provider` (provider_response boundary) or `request` depending on the
provider.

`?` inside encode converts `http::Error`, `serde_json::Error`,
`url::ParseError`, `MessageError` and boxed errors, so the per-site
`map_err` choices are removed. Every helper and rig-to-provider `TryFrom`
conversion called from encode returns `EncodeError`. The driver's own
request-shape failures (a streamed batch, a multipart stream) and
`UnsupportedResponseEncoding`, which is refused before sending, are
request errors too. rig-typesafeai's wire and rig-gemini-grpc's shared
schema conversion follow.

* test(rig-core): pin request-building classification for every encode failure

Every EncodeError constructor and conversion yields a request classification, checked against an exhaustive match on ProviderError. Builder failures and pre-send refusals from the OpenAI chat, Responses and modality wires, Anthropic, Gemini, Cohere, Voyage and Ollama, the driver's two request-shape failures, and rig-typesafeai's wire all report as request failures with a request boundary and no retry.

* test(rig-cassette): expect llama.cpp's specific-tool refusal as a request error

The refusal is raised while encoding, before anything is sent, so it now classifies as a request-building failure. The cells still prove it is rig's own and not the transport error the dead address would produce.

* refactor(rig-core): keep encode error sources and cover the websocket handshake

Review follow-ups. Builder failures in the OpenAI chat and Responses wires,
the Gemini Interactions wires, and the Responses tool-result conversion use
`?`, so the underlying error stays the source instead of being flattened to
text. `From<url::ParseError>` is removed: no encode path parses a URL, and
without it an EncodeError is always a `Request`. The websocket handshake
request is built through EncodeError too, so a bad base URL reports as a
request failure rather than `http` or `provider`. A stale doc comment is
fixed, and rig-gemini-grpc pins its schema-conversion failure.

* refactor(rig-core)!: the sink canonicalizes; the fold collects

block assembly moves into the sink and is private: every `BlockEnd`

input is an error item in its place (`ProviderError::MalformedToolInput`,
whose report is the one the stream carried before); the terminal's
finish reason agrees with the completed tool calls; a second terminal is
dropped; and the text and reasoning blocks still open are closed before
the terminal, at EOF and before a terminal failure (`Sink::finish`).

`Fold::absorb` takes the event by reference. `CompletionFold` collects:
each block from its end, in the order the blocks began, the message id
and the terminal record. `CompletionFold::step` and `Absorbed` are gone;
`CompletionStream` absorbs each event and yields it. Every consumer-side

longer public.

items move with them. No cassette changes.

`Operation::fold(request, wire, mode)` builds the fold for one reply and
has no default: like `Wire::decoder(mode)`, a fold knows the wire and the
mode from birth. `Fold` no longer requires `Default`. `stamp_reply` takes
the `Reply` by reference, `stamp_event` and `record_event` are the
defaulted per-event pair of `stamp_reply` and `record`, and `telemetry`
takes the `Mode` on `Operation` and on `Wire`. `One` is renamed `Events`:
it is the sink every operation but completion uses.

rig-gemini-grpc, rig-fastembed). The driver's unary branch still folds.

* refactor(rig-core)!: Streamed<Op>; call is stream drained; DynModel generic and 'static

One loop consumes the driver's steps. `run` never folds: in both modes it
yields each page's `Opened` (the transport's request id), the decoded
`Event`s, and one `Closed` with the aggregated reply. It keeps what is not
folding: reading a unary page whole, enriching a unary failure, document
reassembly, cursor following with its ceiling and repeated-cursor guard,
and the observation ending (`Decoded`, or the first error) at the decoder.

`Streamed<Op>` (`rig_core::streaming`, with `CompletionStream =
Streamed<Completion>`) is the one type a reply arrives as, for every
operation. Its private `poll_step` is the only place a step is consumed:
it records a page's request id on the span, stamps each event
(`Operation::stamp_event`), records it on a streamed span
(`Operation::record_event`), absorbs it by reference and yields it, and
stamps errors with the request id. `ProviderError` becomes `ErrorReport`
only in its public `Stream` impl. `Model::stream`/`stream_observed` and
`DynModel::stream`/`stream_observed` are generic over the operation, and
`call` is `stream` in unary mode, drained (`Streamed::drain`), then
`accept`.

`ErasedModel` takes `self: Arc<Self>` for `call` and returns a `'static`
future, so `DynModel::call`/`call_observed` can be spawned; `streamed`
replaces `steps`. Deleted: `unary`'s fold, the driver's `fold`, `steps`,
`completion_stream`, the completion-only `Model` block, `Step::Done`, the
`CompletionStream` struct and `CompletionFold::finish_stream`; the
completion fold knows its mode (`CompletionFold::opened(.., mode)`).

A relayed stream's error reports travel as `ProviderError::Relayed`, which
reports as the relayed report unchanged. The HTTP transport reads a
whole-framed reply as a unary one in both modes, so its document is a
fact of the reply streamed or not. Tests: an operation the crate never
heard of calls and streams typed and erased (and a spawned erased call);
a streamed embedding and a streamed paged listing finish to what `call`
gives, with the cursor guards and their warnings.

feat(gemini): automatic explicit caching for long runs (#2628)

* feat(rig-cassette): a recorded clock and a record-only pause

Code whose requests depend on time (a cache expiry, a TTL chosen from the
gaps between calls) must make the same decisions on replay. A session's
CassetteClock reads wall time while recording and saves every reading
beside the fixture as <fixture>.clock.json; replay returns the same
readings in order and panics when the code reads more or fewer.
ProviderCassette::pause sleeps only while recording and refuses anything
over 60 s.

* feat(gemini): opt-in current-turn thought replay

On Gemini 3 every thought signature a request re-sends is expanded back
into the reasoning it came from and billed again as input; no explicit
cache holds it. ThoughtReplay::CurrentTurn leaves signatures out of every
part before the newest user message (the turns the model has finished)
and keeps the current turn's, which Gemini validates. The history is not
modified. The default stays ThoughtReplay::All, as Google's thinking guide
asks; the effect on answer quality is unmeasured.

* feat(gemini): automatic explicit caching as a transport (CacheBook, Caching)

A Caching<T> transport wraps any GenerateContent transport. Each request
passes through it with its encoded body; a shared, content-addressed
CacheBook decides what the request reads from a cache and when a new cache
is worth creating:

- Bodies are parsed with contents kept as raw JSON, digested as a chain
  (model + prefix, then each content's bytes), stripped of what a cache
  holds, and cache bodies are built from the same bytes.
- Auto policy: read the longest live cache the request starts with; accrue
  the premium paid for tokens a cache could have held; roll (cache
  everything but the newest content) once that premium covers the new
  cache's creation and storage; stay inline where implicit caching serves
  or above 16k cacheable tokens until implicit is seen failing; cache a
  prefix two conversations share at once.
- Lifecycle: TTLs follow the gaps between calls (capped at 81 min), a cache
  read near expiry is extended, a replaced or idle conversation cache is
  deleted, an expired cache is never sent, a 403 forgets the cache and
  re-sends inline once, close() deletes everything live.
- Resume: leases() for a checkpoint, restore() and prove() in a new process.
- CacheReport and CacheEvent account for creation, reads and storage.

Model<GenerateContent, T>::caching(&book) builds it; nothing changes
without a book.

* feat(rig-cassette): CassetteClock::pause, so test bodies holding only the clock can pause

* test(cassette): compare a request that reads a Gemini cache as the conversation it stands for

A request that reads an explicit cache sends only what came after it, so
the prefix guard saw it as an unrelated, shorter conversation and skipped
it. splice_cached_content rebuilds the request from the cachedContents body
the same cassette recorded: the cache's system instruction, tools, tool
config and contents, then the request's contents. A roll to a new cache is
then compared as the whole conversation, and a cache that rewrote an
earlier turn is a violation.

* fix(gemini): Usage input includes the hosted-tool prompt

Gemini counts cached tokens against the prompt plus the prompt its own
hosted tools add (toolUsePromptTokenCount), so with hosted tools the
cached count could exceed input_tokens. input_tokens is now
promptTokenCount + toolUsePromptTokenCount, in both unary and streaming
(one conversion). cache_creation_input_tokens stays None: a decoder cannot
know that a transport created a cache; CacheBook::report() accounts for it.

Five code-execution effect goldens change only their input_tokens
(regenerated with cargo xtask cassette goldens); three existing unit
assertions move to prompt + toolUse.

* test(cassette): the prefix guard accepts a finished turn losing its thought signatures

ThoughtReplay::CurrentTurn stops re-sending a turn's signatures once the
next user message arrives, so that turn's bytes change. compare() now
accepts exactly that change: the later content equals the earlier one with
its thoughtSignature keys removed, and a new user message follows it in the
later request. Any other difference, or a signature dropped from the
current turn, is still a moved prefix. No fixture is exempted.

* test(cassette): history-survival checks splice requests that read a Gemini cache

A request that reads an explicit cache sends only the tail after it, so
the pairing check saw function responses without their calls and the
survival check saw signatures vanish. Both now rebuild such a request from
the cachedContents body the same cassette recorded. The four fixtures that
opt into ThoughtReplay::CurrentTurn are exempted for thought_signature
only, with the reason: the opt-in stops re-sending finished turns'
signatures by design.

* test(gemini): live long-run recordings of automatic caching

Nine gemini-3.8-flash runs under fixtures/cassettes/gemini/auto_caching,
each with its recorded clock: 100-turn support chats (current-turn replay,
default replay, streamed, checkpoint and resume, compaction), a 60-call

(too-small cache, expiry across a pause, a cache deleted mid-run, double
close) and a 30-turn uncached baseline. Every book run asserts on its
recorded traffic: nothing a cache holds is re-sent, cache plus tail is the
conversation byte for byte, every cache is deleted, every replaced cache
was read at least three times, cache creation stays under 15% of prompt
tokens, plus each run's thresholds. support_chat_100_auto is not recorded
yet (see the PR body).

check-wires: inside providers/ everything is a wire. The cache book's data,

Caching<T> transport, Model::caching and the book's async prove/close move

equal to the provider's own wherever it reports one. Usage's rustdoc

Every provider's Usage now counts cache reads and writes inside

refactor!: replace NonEmpty<T> with Vec<T>, check empty turns at the request boundary (#2640)

* feat(rig-core): reject empty history and content at the request boundary

#2273 replaced `OneOrMany` with `Vec` and moved its request-direction rule
to `CompletionRequest::validate_message_content`: an empty `chat_history`,
a user or assistant message with no content, or a tool result with no
content blocks is rejected locally, naming the role and index, instead of
becoming a provider 400. #2617 made those lists `NonEmpty` and removed the
check. This restores it ahead of returning the lists to `Vec`.

The check runs at the driver's one entry. `Operation` gains a defaulted
`validate`, which `Model::open` calls before the request is encoded;
`Completion` implements it with `validate_message_content`. So `Model::call`,
`Model::stream`, their `_observed` twins, `DynModel`, every model the bus
serves, and the agent and ECS runtimes built on them are covered without a
second scan. The OpenAI Responses websocket session sends without the
driver and calls the check itself, as it did in 0.42.

The response direction is unchanged: empty assistant content is legal at
the rig level, and each wire still judges its own replies with
`require_non_empty`. `System` content is a `String` and is not checked.

While the lists are still `NonEmpty` the check is redundant for the
completion operation; the driver test proves the hook stops a rejected
request before its transport is called.

* refactor(rig-core)!: replace NonEmpty with Vec

#2617 introduced `NonEmpty<T>` and made `Message::User::content`,
`Message::Assistant::content`, `ToolResult::content` and
`CompletionRequest::chat_history` non-empty by type. #2273, shipped in
0.42.0, had just replaced `OneOrMany<T>` with `Vec<T>` for the same fields
and stated the rule this keeps: an empty request is rejected at the request
boundary, and empty assistant content is legal at the rig level. The
previous commit restored that boundary check; this one returns the fields
to `Vec` and deletes `NonEmpty` and `Empty`.

Relative to 0.42.0 the content and history types are unchanged, so 0.42
users have nothing to migrate for them. Code written against `main`
replaces `NonEmpty::new(x)` with `vec![x]` and drops `rig::NonEmpty` and
`rig::Empty` imports. `ToolCall::result`, `Message::tool_results`,
`UserContent::tool_result` and `ToolOutput::into_content` take or return
`Vec`, as 0.42's constructors did. `From<Vec<Message>> for CompletionRequest`
and `From<Vec<_>> for Message` replace their `NonEmpty` forms.

`NonEmpty` serialized as a plain array, so wire bodies, effect logs,
checkpoints, goldens and cassettes are byte-identical. Deserializing `[]`
succeeds again; sending it fails the request check.

Every site that relied on the type keeps its behaviour with an explicit
check:
- Skip if empty: `CompletionResponse::message`, the agent's partial
  streamed turn, `transcript::assistant_message` and
  `invalid_tool_retry_user_message` still build no message from nothing.
- Error if empty: `ToolOutput::content`, rig-ecs `MessageParts::user` and
  `assistant`, the tool-result read in the content graph and `fold_request`
  keep their errors. Bedrock's reply conversion uses `require_non_empty`
  again, as in 0.42.
- Reads of `first()` handle `None`, or rely on an earlier length or
  emptiness check.

Tests that asserted the type rejects empty input now assert the request
check rejects it. New tests cover each request surface (typed and erased
models, the Responses websocket session, the agent's awaited and streamed
runs and extractor, rig-ecs runs, rig-candle's local wire), the skip-if-empty
sites, and an empty content list that round-trips through serde and is
rejected when sent.

The Frozen API examples use `Vec`: `p4_tools` sends its next turn only when
both the turn and its results are there, and `p5_local_operation` rejects an
empty frame list in `Operation::validate`.
